---
title: "Statistical Distance and Optimal Transport"
---

## Overview

A generative model does not produce a single number that we can compare against
a label. It produces a whole distribution, and training it means making that
distribution resemble the distribution the data came from. So before any
architecture is discussed, we need an answer to a prior question: given two
probability distributions over the same space, what does it mean to say that
one is close to the other, and how close?

This lecture gives two answers, and they are genuinely different. The first
compares distributions pointwise, through the ratio of their densities; this
produces the family of $f$-divergences, of which the Kullback--Leibler and
Jensen--Shannon divergences are the members that generative modelling actually
uses. The second compares them by asking how much work it takes to carry the
mass of one distribution onto the other; this produces optimal transport and
the Wasserstein distances. The distinction is not decorative. We will see that
when two distributions have disjoint supports --- which, for a generative model
of images, is the normal situation rather than an edge case --- every
$f$-divergence is constant and therefore carries no gradient, while the
Wasserstein distance still varies smoothly. That single fact is the reason the
GAN literature moved from the original minimax objective to the Wasserstein
one, and it is the reason this material comes first in the course.

By the end the reader should be able to state and prove what an $f$-divergence
is and when it is finite, derive the Kullback--Leibler and Jensen--Shannon
divergences from their generators, recognise integral probability metrics as
the dual-norm view of the same problem and estimate one of them from samples,
set up both Monge's and Kantorovich's transport problems and say why the first
can fail in three different ways, prove Kantorovich duality in the discrete
case and read off from it both the Kantorovich--Rubinstein form of $W_{1}$ and
the $c$-cyclical monotonicity of optimal plans, and identify the optimal
transport map between two Gaussians as an instance of Brenier's theorem.

This chapter assumes the metric space, convexity and duality material of the
preliminaries chapter and does not restate it.

## Notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}$ | Polish spaces; the data space and the latent space |
| $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})$ | Borel probability measures on $\mathcal{X}$ |
| $\mu, \nu$ | probability measures; $\mu$ is the source, $\nu$ the target |
| $P, Q$ | the same measures when densities or masses are meant |
| $\nu \ll \mu$ | $\nu$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$ |
| $d\nu / d\mu$ | Radon--Nikodym derivative of $\nu$ with respect to $\mu$ |
| $T_{\#}\mu$ | push-forward of $\mu$ under the map $T$ |
| $\Pi(\mu,\nu)$ | couplings of $\mu$ and $\nu$ |
| $c(x,y)$ | transport cost from $x$ to $y$ |
| $\varphi^{c}$ | $c$-transform of the potential $\varphi$ |
| $\mathrm{Lip}_{1}(\mathcal{X})$ | $1$-Lipschitz real functions on $\mathcal{X}$ |
| $G_{\theta}$ | generator with parameters $\theta$ |
| $p_{\text{data}}$ | the unknown data distribution |

Throughout, $\log$ is the natural logarithm and the convention
$0 \log 0 = 0$ is in force, justified by continuity of $t \log t$ at $t = 0$.

## Why the distance between distributions is the question {#sec-why}

Fix a latent space $\mathcal{Y}$ carrying a simple reference measure $\nu$ ---
in practice $\nu = \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ --- and a data space $\mathcal{X}$. A
generator is a measurable map $G_{\theta} : \mathcal{Y} \to \mathcal{X}$. It
does not model a density directly. What it gives us is a procedure for drawing
samples: take $z \sim \nu$ and return $G_{\theta}(z)$. The distribution of the
result is the image of $\nu$ under $G_{\theta}$, written

$$
\mu_{\theta} = G_{\theta \#} \nu ,
$$ {#eq-generator-pushforward}

and made precise in @def-pushforward below and drawn in @fig-pushforward.
Training the generator means
choosing $\theta$ so that $\mu_{\theta}$ resembles $p_{\text{data}}$, which we
only ever see through a finite sample. So we need a function
$D(\mu_{\theta}, p_{\text{data}})$ that is small exactly when the two agree,
and --- this is the part that is easy to forget --- whose gradient in $\theta$
points somewhere useful when they do not.

There is an obstruction, and it is structural rather than accidental. The
support of $\mu_{\theta}$ is contained in $G_{\theta}(\mathcal{Y})$, the image
of a space of dimension $\dim \mathcal{Y}$, which in practice is a hundred or
so. The data are believed to lie near a manifold of similarly low dimension
inside a pixel space of dimension $10^{5}$ or more. Two such sets, both of
measure zero in the ambient space, generically fail to overlap. Any discrepancy
built out of the ratio of two densities is therefore being asked to compare
$0/0$ almost everywhere, and we will prove in @sec-saturation that it responds
by saturating at a constant. Keeping that obstruction in view is what
organises the rest of the chapter.

![The generator as a push-forward. The latent measure $\nu$ on the left is
carried to $\mu_{\theta} = G_{\theta \#} \nu$ on the right; the mass that
$\mu_{\theta}$ assigns to a region $A$ is exactly the mass $\nu$ assigns to the
latent codes that land in $A$. Nothing here requires $G_{\theta}$ to be
invertible.](figures/lec01/jungwoo-ahn-fig2.png){#fig-pushforward width=75%}

## The measure-theoretic minimum {#sec-measure}

This section fixes three definitions that the rest of the chapter uses without
further comment. It is deliberately brief; the preliminaries chapter treats
measure and integration properly.

::: {#def-abs-cont}
## Absolutely continuous measure
Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be measures on a measurable space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F})$.
We say $\nu$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$, written
$\nu \ll \mu$, if $\mu(A) = 0$ implies $\nu(A) = 0$ for every
$A \in \mathcal{F}$.
:::

The condition says that $\nu$ cannot put mass where $\mu$ puts none. It is the
exact hypothesis under which a density of $\nu$ with respect to $\mu$ can
exist, which is the content of the next theorem. @fig-abs-cont contrasts the
two cases.

![Absolute continuity. In (a) the measure $\nu$ charges a region that $\mu$
does not, so no density of $\nu$ against $\mu$ can exist there and
$\nu \not\ll \mu$. In (b) the support of $\nu$ sits inside that of $\mu$ and
$\nu \ll \mu$.](figures/lec01/jungwoo-ahn-fig1.png){#fig-abs-cont width=85%}

::: {#thm-radon-nikodym}
## Radon--Nikodym
Let $\lambda$ and $\nu$ be $\sigma$-finite measures on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F})$
with $\lambda \ll \nu$. Then there is a non-negative $\mathcal{F}$-measurable
function $g$ on $\Omega$, unique up to $\nu$-null sets, such that

$$
\lambda(A) = \int_{A} g \, d\nu , \qquad A \in \mathcal{F} .
$$ {#eq-radon-nikodym}
:::

The function $g$ is written $d\lambda / d\nu$. A proof is given in
@sec-appendix-rn rather than here, because the argument is self-contained but
long enough to interrupt the development. An ordinary probability density
function is the special case $\nu = $ Lebesgue measure: writing $p = dP/dx$
recovers $P(A) = \int_{A} p(x) \, dx$.

::: {#def-pushforward}
## Push-forward of a measure
Let $(\mathcal{X}_{1}, \mathcal{B}_{1})$ and
$(\mathcal{X}_{2}, \mathcal{B}_{2})$ be measurable spaces, $\mu$ a measure on
the first, and $T : \mathcal{X}_{1} \to \mathcal{X}_{2}$ measurable. The
push-forward $T_{\#}\mu$ is the measure on $\mathcal{B}_{2}$ defined by

$$
(T_{\#}\mu)(A) = \mu\bigl(T^{-1}(A)\bigr)
  = \mu\bigl(\{ x : T(x) \in A \}\bigr) .
$$ {#eq-pushforward}
:::

Read @eq-pushforward as a statement about sampling: if $x \sim \mu$ then
$T(x) \sim T_{\#}\mu$. For a generator this is exactly
@eq-generator-pushforward, and it is worth noting what the definition does not
require. There is no inverse of $T$ anywhere in it --- only the preimage of a
set, which exists for any map --- and no density. A generator that collapses a
whole region of latent space to one image is perfectly well described.

The following lemma is used repeatedly and is never stated in the lecture, so
we prove it.

::: {#lem-change-of-variables}
## Change of variables
Let $T : \mathcal{X}_{1} \to \mathcal{X}_{2}$ be measurable and let
$h : \mathcal{X}_{2} \to [0, \infty]$ be measurable. Then

$$
\int_{\mathcal{X}_{2}} h \, d(T_{\#}\mu)
  = \int_{\mathcal{X}_{1}} (h \circ T) \, d\mu .
$$ {#eq-change-of-variables}
:::

::: {.proof}
Take first $h = \mathbf{1}_{A}$ for $A \in \mathcal{B}_{2}$. The left-hand side
is $(T_{\#}\mu)(A)$, which is $\mu(T^{-1}(A))$ by @eq-pushforward. The
right-hand side is $\int \mathbf{1}_{A}(T(x)) \, d\mu(x)$, and
$\mathbf{1}_{A}(T(x)) = \mathbf{1}_{T^{-1}(A)}(x)$, so it is also
$\mu(T^{-1}(A))$. The two sides agree.

By linearity of the integral they agree for non-negative simple functions. For
general measurable $h \geq 0$ choose simple $h_{n} \uparrow h$ pointwise; then
$h_{n} \circ T \uparrow h \circ T$ pointwise, and monotone convergence applied
on each side gives the result. An integrable $h$ of arbitrary sign follows by
splitting into $h^{+}$ and $h^{-}$.
:::

In particular, taking $h$ to be a cost function turns an integral against a
push-forward measure into an integral against the original one; this is the
step that makes Monge's problem in @sec-monge computable at all.

## Metrics and divergences are not the same thing {#sec-metric-divergence}

::: {#def-metric-axioms}
## Metric
A metric on a set $\mathcal{X}$ is a function
$d : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}_{+}$ such that for all
$x, y, z \in \mathcal{X}$:

1. $d(x,y) \geq 0$;
2. $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$;
3. $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$;
4. $d(x,z) \leq d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.
:::

::: {#def-divergence}
## Divergence
A divergence on $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})$ is a function
$D : \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}) \times \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}) \to [0, \infty]$
satisfying only conditions 1 and 2 of @def-metric-axioms. Symmetry and the triangle
inequality are not required.
:::

The distinction is exactly what separates the two halves of this chapter. The
$f$-divergences of @sec-f-divergences satisfy only the first two conditions:
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P \Vert Q)$ and $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q \Vert P)$ are different
numbers, and there is no triangle inequality relating three distributions. The
Wasserstein distance of @sec-wasserstein satisfies all four and is a metric in
the full sense --- we prove this as @thm-wp-metric. Statistical distances thus
split into a divergence branch, which leads to the GAN and $f$-GAN objectives,
and a metric branch, which leads to W-GAN.

One more definition from the preliminaries is needed later, in the
Kantorovich--Rubinstein theorem.

::: {#def-lipschitz}
## Lipschitz continuity
Given metric spaces $(\mathcal{X}, d_{\mathcal{X}})$ and
$(\mathcal{Y}, d_{\mathcal{Y}})$, a function
$f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}$ is Lipschitz continuous with constant
$K \geq 0$ if
$d_{\mathcal{Y}}(f(x_{1}), f(x_{2})) \leq K \, d_{\mathcal{X}}(x_{1}, x_{2})$
for all $x_{1}, x_{2} \in \mathcal{X}$. We write
$\mathrm{Lip}_{1}(\mathcal{X})$ for the real-valued functions on $\mathcal{X}$
that are Lipschitz with constant $1$.
:::

## Divergences generated by a convex function {#sec-f-divergences}

The first family of statistical distances compares $P$ and $Q$ through the
ratio of their densities, passed through a convex function.

::: {#def-f-divergence}
## f-divergence
Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on a space $\Omega$ with
$\mu \ll \nu$, and let $f$ be a convex function with $f(1) = 0$. The
$f$-divergence of $\mu$ from $\nu$ is

$$
D_{f}(\mu \Vert \nu)
  := \int_{\Omega} f\!\left( \frac{d\mu}{d\nu} \right) d\nu .
$$ {#eq-f-divergence}

If $\mu \ll \xi$ and $\nu \ll \xi$ for a common measure $\xi$ on $\Omega$,
with densities $p = d\mu/d\xi$ and $q = d\nu/d\xi$, this reads

$$
D_{f}(P \Vert Q)
  := \int_{\Omega} f\!\left( \frac{p(x)}{q(x)} \right) q(x) \, d\xi(x) ,
$$ {#eq-f-divergence-density}

and in the discrete case, with $P$ and $Q$ probability mass functions,

$$
D_{f}(P \Vert Q) := \sum_{x} Q(x) \, f\!\left( \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} \right) .
$$ {#eq-f-divergence-discrete}
:::

Two features of @eq-f-divergence are worth naming before we go on, because
both come back later. The integration is against the *second* argument, and
the ratio is of the first to the second; swapping $P$ and $Q$ therefore gives a
different number in general. And the definition presupposes $\mu \ll \nu$, so
that $d\mu/d\nu$ exists at all by @thm-radon-nikodym. When that fails,
@eq-f-divergence is not repaired by any pointwise convention: the standard
extension splits $\mu$ into its absolutely continuous and singular parts and
charges the singular part at the recession slope of $f$, which is
@eq-f-divergence-general below. Finiteness then depends on $f$ at both ends,
on $f(0)$ as well as on $\lim_{u \to \infty} f(u)/u$, and not on growth alone:
reverse Kullback--Leibler has recession slope $0$ and is still $+\infty$ on
singular pairs, because $f(0) = +\infty$. This is the seed of
@sec-saturation.

The requirement $f(1) = 0$ is a normalisation, and convexity is what makes the
whole family well behaved:

::: {#prp-f-nonneg}
## Non-negativity
For any convex $f$ with $f(1) = 0$, $D_{f}(P \Vert Q) \geq 0$. If in addition
$f$ is strictly convex at $1$, then $D_{f}(P \Vert Q) = 0$ if and only if
$P = Q$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Write the divergence as an expectation under $Q$ of the random variable
$U = p(X)/q(X)$, with $X \sim Q$:

$$
D_{f}(P \Vert Q) = \mathbb{E}_{Q}\bigl[ f(U) \bigr] .
$$

Since $f$ is convex, Jensen's inequality gives
$\mathbb{E}_{Q}[f(U)] \geq f(\mathbb{E}_{Q}[U])$. The expectation inside is

$$
\mathbb{E}_{Q}[U]
  = \int \frac{p(x)}{q(x)} \, q(x) \, d\xi(x)
  = \int p(x) \, d\xi(x) = 1 ,
$$

because $p$ is a probability density. Hence
$D_{f}(P \Vert Q) \geq f(1) = 0$, which is the first claim.

For the second, suppose $D_{f}(P \Vert Q) = 0$. Convexity supplies a
supporting line at $u = 1$: there is $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with
$f(u) \geq f(1) + a(u-1) = a(u-1)$ for every $u > 0$. Since
$\mathbb{E}_{Q}[U] = 1$, subtracting that line changes nothing:

$$
0 = D_{f}(P \Vert Q) = \mathbb{E}_{Q}\bigl[ f(U) \bigr]
  = \mathbb{E}_{Q}\bigl[ f(U) - a(U-1) \bigr] ,
$$

and the integrand is non-negative. A non-negative random variable with zero
expectation vanishes almost surely, so $f(U) = a(U-1)$ $Q$-almost surely. If
$f$ is strictly convex at $1$ the supporting line meets the graph only at
$u = 1$, so $U = 1$ $Q$-almost surely; that is, $p = q$ almost everywhere and
$P = Q$. Conversely if $P = Q$ then $U \equiv 1$
and the integrand is $f(1) = 0$ everywhere.
:::

Choosing $f$ selects a member of the family.

| Divergence | Generator $f(u)$ | Symmetric | Bounded |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kullback--Leibler | $u \log u$ | no | no |
| Reverse Kullback--Leibler | $-\log u$ | no | no |
| Pearson $\chi^{2}$ | $(u-1)^{2}$ | no | no |
| Squared Hellinger | $(\sqrt{u} - 1)^{2}$ | yes | yes, by $2$ |
| Total variation | $\tfrac{1}{2}\lvert u - 1 \rvert$ | yes | yes, by $1$ |
| Jensen--Shannon | $(u+1)\log\frac{2}{u+1} + u \log u$ | yes | yes, by $2\log 2$ |

### Kullback--Leibler divergence

Take $f(t) = t \log t$, which is convex on $(0,\infty)$ and vanishes at
$t = 1$. Substituting into @eq-f-divergence-discrete,

$$
\begin{aligned}
  D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P \Vert Q)
    &= \sum_{x} Q(x) \, \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} \log \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} \\
    &= \sum_{x} P(x) \log \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} \\
    &= \sum_{x} P(x) \log P(x) \; - \; \sum_{x} P(x) \log Q(x) \\
    &= H(P,Q) - H(P) ,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-kl-entropy}

where the cancellation in the second line is legitimate wherever $Q(x) > 0$,
and the terms with $P(x) = 0$ contribute nothing under the convention
$0 \log 0 = 0$. The entropy and cross-entropy appearing in @eq-kl-entropy are

$$
H(P) = - \sum_{x} P(x) \log P(x) ,
\qquad
H(P,Q) = - \sum_{x} P(x) \log Q(x) .
$$ {#eq-entropies}

@eq-kl-entropy is why $D_{\mathrm{KL}}$ is also called the relative entropy: it
is the excess in the average number of nats needed to describe samples from
$P$ using a code built for $Q$, over the best code for $P$ itself. It also
explains why minimising a cross-entropy loss over $\theta$ and minimising
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P \Vert Q_{\theta})$ are the same problem --- $H(P)$ does not
depend on $\theta$.

Note where @eq-kl-entropy breaks. If there is a point with $P(x) > 0$ and
$Q(x) = 0$ then the ratio is infinite and $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P \Vert Q) = +\infty$:
the generator $f(t) = t\log t$ satisfies $f(t)/t \to \infty$. So
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}$ is finite only when $P \ll Q$, which is precisely the
hypothesis of @def-f-divergence and, as we will see, precisely what a
generative model cannot guarantee.

Taking $f(u) = -\log u$ instead gives

$$
D_{f}(P \Vert Q) = \sum_{x} Q(x) \log \frac{Q(x)}{P(x)}
  = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q \Vert P) ,
$$ {#eq-reverse-kl}

the reverse Kullback--Leibler divergence, finite only when $Q \ll P$. The
asymmetry is not a technicality: minimising $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P \Vert Q_\theta)$
over $\theta$ penalises putting no mass where $P$ has some, so the fitted model
spreads out to cover every mode; minimising
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q_{\theta} \Vert P)$ penalises putting mass where $P$ has
none, so the fitted model contracts onto one mode and ignores the rest.
@fig-kl-directions shows the two fits side by side.

![Mass-covering versus mode-seeking. A unimodal $Q_{\theta}$ is fitted to a
bimodal $P$ under the two orderings of the Kullback--Leibler divergence.
Minimising $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P \Vert Q_{\theta})$ forces $Q_{\theta}$ to cover
both modes and so to place mass in the valley between them; minimising
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q_{\theta} \Vert P)$ lets it lock onto a single mode. This is
the divergence-level description of mode
collapse.](figures/lec01/jungwoo-ahn-fig4.png){#fig-kl-directions width=85%}

### Total variation

The generator $f(u) = \tfrac{1}{2}\lvert u - 1 \rvert$ is convex and vanishes
at $u = 1$, so it defines an $f$-divergence. It is the one member of the family
that is also a metric, and the one that will reappear in @sec-ipm from the
other direction entirely.

::: {#prp-tv}
## Total variation
With $f(u) = \tfrac{1}{2}\lvert u-1 \rvert$,

$$
D_{f}(P \Vert Q)
  = \tfrac{1}{2} \int \lvert p(x) - q(x) \rvert \, d\xi(x)
  = \sup_{A} \, \lvert P(A) - Q(A) \rvert
  =: \delta(P,Q) ,
$$ {#eq-tv}

the supremum being over measurable sets $A$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The first equality is immediate from @eq-f-divergence-density:

$$
\int \tfrac{1}{2} \left\lvert \frac{p}{q} - 1 \right\rvert q \, d\xi
  = \tfrac{1}{2} \int \lvert p - q \rvert \, d\xi .
$$

For the second, write $r = p - q$ and let $A^{\ast} = \{ x : p(x) > q(x) \}$.
Since $P$ and $Q$ are probability measures, $\int r \, d\xi = 0$, so

$$
\int_{A^{\ast}} r \, d\xi = - \int_{(A^{\ast})^{c}} r \, d\xi
  = \int_{(A^{\ast})^{c}} \lvert r \rvert \, d\xi .
$$

The integrand $\lvert r \rvert$ equals $r$ on $A^{\ast}$ and $-r$ off it, so

$$
\int \lvert r \rvert \, d\xi
  = \int_{A^{\ast}} r \, d\xi + \int_{(A^{\ast})^{c}} \lvert r \rvert \, d\xi
  = 2 \int_{A^{\ast}} r \, d\xi ,
$$

giving $P(A^{\ast}) - Q(A^{\ast}) = \tfrac{1}{2}\int \lvert r \rvert \, d\xi$.
That attains the supremum. For the upper bound, any measurable $A$ satisfies

$$
\lvert P(A) - Q(A) \rvert = \left\lvert \int_{A} r \, d\xi \right\rvert
  \leq \max\left\{ \int_{A} r^{+} d\xi , \int_{A} r^{-} d\xi \right\}
  \leq \int r^{+} d\xi
  = \tfrac{1}{2} \int \lvert r \rvert \, d\xi ,
$$

where the last equality uses $\int r^{+} d\xi = \int r^{-} d\xi$, itself a
restatement of $\int r \, d\xi = 0$.
:::

Unlike the Kullback--Leibler divergence, @eq-tv never exceeds $1$ and never
needs absolute continuity: the generator $\tfrac{1}{2}\lvert u-1 \rvert$ grows
linearly, so $f(u)/u$ stays bounded. Boundedness will turn out to be exactly
the problem rather than the cure.

### Jensen--Shannon divergence

The Jensen--Shannon divergence symmetrises the Kullback--Leibler divergence by
comparing both arguments against their average.

::: {#def-js}
## Jensen--Shannon divergence
For probability measures $P$ and $Q$, set $M = \tfrac{1}{2}(P + Q)$. Then

$$
D_{\mathrm{JS}}(P \Vert Q)
  := \tfrac{1}{2} D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P \Vert M)
   + \tfrac{1}{2} D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q \Vert M) .
$$ {#eq-js}
:::

Symmetry is immediate, since $M$ is unchanged by swapping $P$ and $Q$. The
substantive point is that @eq-js is always finite, which the
Kullback--Leibler divergence is not.

::: {#lem-js-well-defined}
## The mixture dominates both arguments
$P \ll M$ and $Q \ll M$, so both Radon--Nikodym derivatives $dP/dM$ and
$dQ/dM$ exist and @eq-js is well defined for every pair $P, Q$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $A$ be measurable with $M(A) = 0$. By definition of $M$,

$$
0 = M(A) = \tfrac{1}{2} P(A) + \tfrac{1}{2} Q(A) .
$$

Both $P(A) \geq 0$ and $Q(A) \geq 0$, and a sum of non-negative terms vanishes
only if each vanishes, so $P(A) = Q(A) = 0$. By @def-abs-cont this is exactly
$P \ll M$ and $Q \ll M$.
:::

This is the whole advantage over the Kullback--Leibler divergence. To use
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P \Vert Q)$ we must know in advance that $P \ll Q$, which for
a model distribution and an unknown data distribution we never do.

::: {#prp-js-bounded}
## Jensen--Shannon is bounded
$0 \leq D_{\mathrm{JS}}(P \Vert Q) \leq \log 2$, with the upper bound attained
exactly when $P$ and $Q$ are mutually singular.
:::

::: {.proof}
The lower bound is @prp-f-nonneg. For the upper bound, note that pointwise
$M = \tfrac{1}{2}(P+Q) \geq \tfrac{1}{2}P$ as measures, so $dP/dM \leq 2$
$M$-almost everywhere. Hence

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P \Vert M) = \int \log\!\left( \frac{dP}{dM} \right) dP
  \leq \int \log 2 \, dP = \log 2 ,
$$

and the same bound holds for $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q \Vert M)$. Substituting both
into @eq-js gives $D_{\mathrm{JS}} \leq \tfrac{1}{2}\log 2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\log 2
= \log 2$.

Equality requires $dP/dM = 2$ $P$-almost everywhere. Because $P + Q = 2M$,
the two derivatives satisfy $dP/dM + dQ/dM = 2$ $M$-almost everywhere, so on
the set $S = \{ dP/dM = 2 \}$ we have $dQ/dM = 0$ and therefore

$$
Q(S) = \int_{S} \frac{dQ}{dM} \, dM = 0 ,
$$

while $P(S) = 1$. So $P$ and $Q$ are carried by the disjoint sets $S$ and
$S^{c}$, which is mutual singularity.
Conversely, if $P$ and $Q$ live on disjoint sets $S$ and $S^{c}$, then on $S$
we have $M = \tfrac{1}{2}P$ and $dP/dM = 2$, and symmetrically on $S^{c}$,
so both divergences equal $\log 2$.
:::

Finally we connect @eq-js back to @def-f-divergence, and here the lecture's two
slides do not quite agree with each other.

::: {#prp-js-generator}
## The Jensen--Shannon generator carries a factor of two
Let $f_{\mathrm{JS}}(u) = (u+1)\log\frac{2}{u+1} + u \log u$. Then
$f_{\mathrm{JS}}$ is convex with $f_{\mathrm{JS}}(1) = 0$, and

$$
D_{f_{\mathrm{JS}}}(P \Vert Q) = 2 \, D_{\mathrm{JS}}(P \Vert Q) .
$$ {#eq-js-factor}
:::

::: {.proof}
That $f_{\mathrm{JS}}(1) = 2\log 1 + 1 \cdot \log 1 = 0$ is direct. For
convexity, differentiate twice on $u > 0$:

$$
f_{\mathrm{JS}}'(u) = \log \frac{2}{u+1} - 1 + \log u + 1
  = \log \frac{2u}{u+1} ,
\qquad
f_{\mathrm{JS}}''(u) = \frac{1}{u} - \frac{1}{u+1} = \frac{1}{u(u+1)} > 0 .
$$

For the identity, substitute into @eq-f-divergence-discrete with $u = P(x)/Q(x)$ and
clear denominators:

$$
\begin{aligned}
  D_{f_{\mathrm{JS}}}(P \Vert Q)
    &= \sum_{x} Q \left[
         \left( \frac{P}{Q} + 1 \right) \log \frac{2}{\frac{P}{Q} + 1}
         + \frac{P}{Q} \log \frac{P}{Q} \right] \\
    &= \sum_{x} \left[ (P + Q) \log \frac{2Q}{P + Q}
         + P \log \frac{P}{Q} \right] .
\end{aligned}
$$

Now $M = \tfrac{1}{2}(P+Q)$ gives $\dfrac{2Q}{P+Q} = \dfrac{Q}{M}$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
  D_{f_{\mathrm{JS}}}(P \Vert Q)
    &= \sum_{x} \left[ P \log \frac{Q}{M} + Q \log \frac{Q}{M}
         + P \log \frac{P}{Q} \right] \\
    &= \sum_{x} \left[ P \log \!\left( \frac{Q}{M} \cdot \frac{P}{Q} \right)
         + Q \log \frac{Q}{M} \right] \\
    &= \sum_{x} P \log \frac{P}{M} + \sum_{x} Q \log \frac{Q}{M} \\
    &= D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P \Vert M) + D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q \Vert M) ,
\end{aligned}
$$

which by @eq-js is $2 D_{\mathrm{JS}}(P \Vert Q)$.
:::

The factor of two is not an error in either statement; it is a collision of two
conventions. @eq-js is the information-theoretic normalisation, under which the
divergence is bounded by $\log 2$ and equals the mutual information between a
sample and a fair coin choosing which of $P$ and $Q$ produced it.
$f_{\mathrm{JS}}$ is the generator tabulated in the $f$-GAN literature, which
omits the $\tfrac{1}{2}$ so that the associated variational objective matches
the original GAN loss up to an additive $\log 4$. **This chapter uses
@eq-js throughout**, so that the bound of @prp-js-bounded reads $\log 2$; a
reader comparing against a table of $f$-divergence generators should expect the
other normalisation and divide by two.

## Disjoint supports and the vanishing gradient {#sec-saturation}

Everything so far has quietly assumed that the density ratio $p/q$ means
something. This section shows what happens when it does not, which for
generative models is the typical case rather than a pathology. The conclusion
is that every $f$-divergence saturates at a constant that does not depend on
how far apart the two distributions are, and that a constant has no gradient.

To say this cleanly we need the standard extension of @def-f-divergence to
pairs that are not absolutely continuous. Let $P = P^{\mathrm{ac}} + P^{\perp}$
be the Lebesgue decomposition of $P$ with respect to $Q$, and define the
recession slope

$$
f'(\infty) := \lim_{u \to \infty} \frac{f(u)}{u} \in (-\infty, +\infty] ,
$$ {#eq-recession}

which exists in the extended reals because $f$ is convex. The $f$-divergence is
then

$$
D_{f}(P \Vert Q)
  := \int f\!\left( \frac{dP^{\mathrm{ac}}}{dQ} \right) dQ
   \; + \; f'(\infty) \, P^{\perp}(\Omega) ,
$$ {#eq-f-divergence-general}

which agrees with @eq-f-divergence when $P \ll Q$, since then
$P^{\perp} = 0$.

::: {#thm-saturation}
## Saturation on disjoint supports
Let $P$ and $Q$ be mutually singular probability measures, written
$P \perp Q$. Then for every generator $f$,

$$
D_{f}(P \Vert Q) = f(0) + f'(\infty) ,
$$ {#eq-saturation}

a constant depending only on $f$ and not on $P$ or $Q$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Mutual singularity means there is a measurable set $S$ with $P(S) = 1$ and
$Q(S) = 0$. Then $P$ is carried by $S$ and $Q$ by $S^{c}$, so the Lebesgue
decomposition of $P$ with respect to $Q$ is $P^{\mathrm{ac}} = 0$ and
$P^{\perp} = P$, whence $dP^{\mathrm{ac}}/dQ = 0$ $Q$-almost everywhere.
Substituting into @eq-f-divergence-general,

$$
D_{f}(P \Vert Q)
  = \int f(0) \, dQ + f'(\infty) \, P(\Omega)
  = f(0) \cdot 1 + f'(\infty) \cdot 1 ,
$$

since $P$ and $Q$ are probability measures.
:::

Evaluating @eq-saturation for the generators tabulated earlier gives the
saturation values directly, and they agree with the bounds proved above.

| Divergence | $f(0)$ | $f'(\infty)$ | Value when $P \perp Q$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kullback--Leibler | $0$ | $+\infty$ | $+\infty$ |
| Reverse Kullback--Leibler | $+\infty$ | $0$ | $+\infty$ |
| Pearson $\chi^{2}$ | $1$ | $+\infty$ | $+\infty$ |
| Squared Hellinger | $1$ | $1$ | $2$ |
| Total variation | $\tfrac{1}{2}$ | $\tfrac{1}{2}$ | $1$ |
| Jensen--Shannon (as $f_{\mathrm{JS}}$) | $\log 2$ | $\log 2$ | $2 \log 2$ |

The last row is a useful consistency check on @prp-js-generator: dividing the
saturation value $2 \log 2$ by the factor of two recovers exactly the bound
$\log 2$ of @prp-js-bounded, attained precisely on mutually singular pairs.
The Pearson $\chi^{2}$ row is the one generator the chapter tabulates but never
works through; @sec-adv-chi2 does so.

### What this costs a generator

::: {#exm-parallel-lines}
## Two parallel segments
Let $Z \sim \mathrm{Uniform}[0,1]$ and work in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$. Define
$\mu_{0}$ to be the law of $(0, Z)$ and, for $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$, define
$\mu_{\theta}$ to be the law of $(\theta, Z)$. Each is uniform on a vertical
unit segment, and for $\theta \neq 0$ the two segments are disjoint. Then

$$
W_{1}(\mu_{0}, \mu_{\theta}) = \lvert \theta \rvert ,
\qquad
D_{\mathrm{JS}}(\mu_{0} \Vert \mu_{\theta}) =
  \begin{cases} \log 2 , & \theta \neq 0 \\ 0 , & \theta = 0 \end{cases} ,
$$

$$
\delta(\mu_{0}, \mu_{\theta}) =
  \begin{cases} 1 , & \theta \neq 0 \\ 0 , & \theta = 0 \end{cases} ,
\qquad
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu_{0} \Vert \mu_{\theta}) =
  \begin{cases} +\infty , & \theta \neq 0 \\ 0 , & \theta = 0 . \end{cases}
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
For $\theta \neq 0$ the supports are the disjoint segments
$\{0\} \times [0,1]$ and $\{\theta\} \times [0,1]$, so
$\mu_{0} \perp \mu_{\theta}$ and the last three claims are
@thm-saturation read off the table, with the Jensen--Shannon entry divided by
two to match the normalisation of @eq-js. At $\theta = 0$ the two measures
coincide and every divergence vanishes by @prp-f-nonneg.

For $W_{1}$, whose definition is @def-wasserstein below, take the coupling
$\pi$ induced by the map $(0,z) \mapsto (\theta, z)$, that is, the law of
$\bigl( (0,Z), (\theta,Z) \bigr)$. Its marginals are $\mu_{0}$ and
$\mu_{\theta}$ by construction, and its cost is

$$
\mathbb{E} \left\lVert (0,Z) - (\theta,Z) \right\rVert
  = \mathbb{E} \lvert \theta \rvert = \lvert \theta \rvert ,
$$

so $W_{1}(\mu_{0}, \mu_{\theta}) \leq \lvert \theta \rvert$. Conversely, let
$\pi$ be any coupling and let $(X, Y) \sim \pi$. Writing $X_{1}, Y_{1}$ for
first coordinates, $X_{1} = 0$ almost surely and $Y_{1} = \theta$ almost
surely, so $\lVert X - Y \rVert \geq \lvert X_{1} - Y_{1} \rvert =
\lvert \theta \rvert$ pointwise, and taking expectations gives
$\mathbb{E}\lVert X - Y \rVert \geq \lvert \theta \rvert$. Hence
$W_{1}(\mu_{0}, \mu_{\theta}) \geq \lvert \theta \rvert$, and the two bounds
agree.
:::

![The four discrepancies of @exm-parallel-lines as functions of the
displacement $\theta$ between two parallel unit segments in the plane. The
Wasserstein distance is the only one that varies with $\theta$; the
Jensen--Shannon divergence and the total variation jump to their saturation
values the instant the supports separate and stay there, and the
Kullback--Leibler divergence is infinite throughout. A gradient step on any
curve but the first has nothing to
follow.](figures/lec01/jungwoo-ahn-fig3.png){#fig-saturation width=85%}

@fig-saturation is the picture to keep. Suppose we train a generator whose only
parameter is the horizontal offset $\theta$, and we descend the divergence in
$\theta$. Under $W_{1}$ the objective is $\lvert \theta \rvert$, with
derivative $\mathrm{sign}(\theta)$: from any starting point the gradient points
at the answer. Under the Jensen--Shannon divergence the objective is the
constant $\log 2$ for every $\theta \neq 0$, so its derivative is zero
everywhere except at the single point we are trying to find. The optimiser
receives no information at all. Under the Kullback--Leibler divergence the
objective is not even finite.

This is not an artefact of a one-dimensional toy. By
@eq-generator-pushforward the model distribution $\mu_{\theta}$ is supported on
$G_{\theta}(\mathcal{Y})$, the image of a latent space of dimension perhaps
$100$, embedded in a pixel space of dimension perhaps $10^{5}$; and the data
are taken to lie on a manifold of comparably small dimension. Two sets of
dimension $100$ inside $\mathbb{R}^{10^{5}}$ that are not deliberately arranged
to meet will be mutually singular, so @thm-saturation applies at essentially
every $\theta$, not just at isolated ones. A generator trained against an
$f$-divergence is therefore relying on the discriminator never becoming very
good --- an unstable thing to rely on, and the observed behaviour of the
original GAN.

Two escapes exist. One is to stop comparing densities pointwise and start
comparing expectations of test functions, which is @sec-ipm. The other is to
measure how far mass must physically move, which is @sec-monge onwards. They
turn out to be the same escape, and they meet in @thm-kantorovich-rubinstein.

## Integral probability metrics {#sec-ipm}

An $f$-divergence asks how the two distributions differ at each point. An
integral probability metric asks instead how differently they answer a
restricted set of questions.

::: {#def-ipm}
## Integral probability metric
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a class of real measurable functions on $\mathcal{X}$. The
integral probability metric associated with $\mathcal{F}$ is

$$
d_{\mathcal{F}}(\mu, \nu)
  := \sup_{h \in \mathcal{F}} \left\lvert
       \int_{\mathcal{X}} h \, d\mu - \int_{\mathcal{X}} h \, d\nu
     \right\rvert .
$$ {#eq-ipm}
:::

The name "dual-norm view" comes from reading @eq-ipm as a norm on the signed
measure $\mu - \nu$. Probability measures pair with bounded functions by
integration, so $\mu - \nu$ acts as a linear functional on the space of test
functions; @eq-ipm is the operator norm of that functional, measured over the
unit ball $\mathcal{F}$. Different choices of $\mathcal{F}$ are different
norms on the same object, and, as we are about to see, three familiar
quantities are three choices. How literally that dual-norm reading may be
taken, and which topology each choice induces, are examined in
@sec-adv-dualnorm.

Throughout we take $\mathcal{F}$ symmetric, $\mathcal{F} = -\mathcal{F}$, as
all three classes below are; the absolute value in @eq-ipm may then be dropped,
since $h$ and $-h$ both compete in the supremum.

::: {#prp-ipm-metric}
## Integral probability metrics are pseudo-metrics
Let every $h \in \mathcal{F}$ be integrable with respect to both measures.
Then $d_{\mathcal{F}}$ is non-negative, symmetric, vanishes when
$\mu = \nu$, and satisfies the triangle inequality. It
is a metric on $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})$ if and only if $\mathcal{F}$ is
measure-determining, meaning that $\int h \, d\mu = \int h \, d\nu$ for all
$h \in \mathcal{F}$ implies $\mu = \nu$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Non-negativity is clear, as is $d_{\mathcal{F}}(\mu,\mu) = 0$. Symmetry holds
because the absolute value is unchanged when $\mu$ and $\nu$ are exchanged.
For the triangle inequality, fix $h \in \mathcal{F}$ and any third measure
$\rho$; then

$$
\left\lvert \int h \, d\mu - \int h \, d\nu \right\rvert
  \leq \left\lvert \int h \, d\mu - \int h \, d\rho \right\rvert
     + \left\lvert \int h \, d\rho - \int h \, d\nu \right\rvert
  \leq d_{\mathcal{F}}(\mu,\rho) + d_{\mathcal{F}}(\rho,\nu) .
$$

The right-hand side does not depend on $h$, so taking the supremum over
$h \in \mathcal{F}$ on the left preserves the inequality.

Finally, $d_{\mathcal{F}}(\mu,\nu) = 0$ says exactly that
$\int h \, d\mu = \int h \, d\nu$ for every $h \in \mathcal{F}$. That this
forces $\mu = \nu$ is the definition of measure-determining, so the second
axiom of @def-metric-axioms holds precisely under that hypothesis.
:::

Note how little was needed: no density ratio, no absolute continuity, and no
common dominating measure. This is why integral probability metrics survive the
situation that defeats @sec-saturation.

### Three instances

**Total variation.** Take $\mathcal{F}$ to be the indicators
$\{ \mathbf{1}_{A} : A \text{ measurable} \}$. Then
$\int \mathbf{1}_{A} d\mu - \int \mathbf{1}_{A} d\nu = \mu(A) - \nu(A)$, so
@eq-ipm reduces to $\sup_{A} \lvert \mu(A) - \nu(A) \rvert$, which is
$\delta(\mu,\nu)$ by @prp-tv. Taking instead the sup-norm ball
$\{ h : \lVert h \rVert_{\infty} \leq 1 \}$ gives $2\delta(\mu,\nu)$, since the
supremum is attained at $h = \mathrm{sign}(p - q)$.

So total variation belongs to both families. That is not a coincidence about
our proof, and it is essentially the only overlap: up to a constant multiple,
total variation is the unique non-trivial statistical distance that is both an
$f$-divergence and an integral probability metric, as @fig-families records.

![The two families of statistical distances and what lies in each. Every
$f$-divergence saturates on disjoint supports by @thm-saturation; the integral
probability metrics on the right need no density ratio and need not saturate.
Total variation is essentially the only member of
both.](figures/lec01/jungwoo-ahn-fig5.png){#fig-families width=75%}

**Wasserstein-1.** Take $\mathcal{F} = \mathrm{Lip}_{1}(\mathcal{X})$ from
@def-lipschitz. The resulting integral probability metric is $W_{1}$. This is
the Kantorovich--Rubinstein theorem and it is genuinely a theorem rather than a
definition, because $W_{1}$ is defined in @def-wasserstein as an infimum over
couplings with no test functions in sight. We prove it as
@thm-kantorovich-rubinstein, once duality is available.

**Maximum mean discrepancy.** Let $k$ be a positive-definite kernel on
$\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{H}_{k}$ its reproducing kernel Hilbert space, so
that $h(x) = \langle h, k(\cdot, x) \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{k}}$ for every
$h \in \mathcal{H}_{k}$. Take $\mathcal{F}$ to be the unit ball
$\{ h : \lVert h \rVert_{\mathcal{H}_{k}} \leq 1 \}$.

::: {#prp-mmd}
## Maximum mean discrepancy
Assume $\int \sqrt{k(x,x)} \, d\mu(x)$ and $\int \sqrt{k(y,y)} \, d\nu(y)$ are
finite, and define the mean embeddings
$m_{\mu} = \int k(\cdot, x) \, d\mu(x)$ and
$m_{\nu} = \int k(\cdot, y) \, d\nu(y)$ in $\mathcal{H}_{k}$. Then

$$
\mathrm{MMD}(\mu,\nu)
  := d_{\mathcal{F}}(\mu,\nu)
   = \lVert m_{\mu} - m_{\nu} \rVert_{\mathcal{H}_{k}} ,
$$ {#eq-mmd}

and

$$
\mathrm{MMD}^{2}(\mu,\nu)
  = \mathbb{E}_{x,x' \sim \mu} k(x,x')
  - 2 \, \mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mu, \, y \sim \nu} k(x,y)
  + \mathbb{E}_{y,y' \sim \nu} k(y,y') .
$$ {#eq-mmd-expanded}
:::

::: {.proof}
By the reproducing property and the finiteness assumption, integration against
$\mu$ is an inner product with the mean embedding:

$$
\int h \, d\mu
  = \int \langle h, k(\cdot,x) \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{k}} \, d\mu(x)
  = \left\langle h, \int k(\cdot,x) \, d\mu(x) \right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{k}}
  = \langle h, m_{\mu} \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{k}} ,
$$

the exchange of integral and inner product being justified by the same
finiteness assumption. Subtracting the same identity for $\nu$,

$$
\int h \, d\mu - \int h \, d\nu
  = \langle h, m_{\mu} - m_{\nu} \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{k}} .
$$

Taking the supremum of the absolute value over the unit ball is the definition
of the dual norm in a Hilbert space, which by Cauchy--Schwarz equals
$\lVert m_{\mu} - m_{\nu} \rVert_{\mathcal{H}_{k}}$, attained at
$h = (m_{\mu} - m_{\nu}) / \lVert m_{\mu} - m_{\nu} \rVert$. That is
@eq-mmd.

For @eq-mmd-expanded, expand the squared norm and use the reproducing property
once more:

$$
\langle m_{\mu}, m_{\nu} \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{k}}
  = \left\langle \int k(\cdot,x) d\mu(x), \int k(\cdot,y) d\nu(y)
    \right\rangle
  = \int \!\! \int \langle k(\cdot,x), k(\cdot,y) \rangle \, d\mu \, d\nu
  = \int \!\! \int k(x,y) \, d\mu \, d\nu ,
$$

and similarly for $\langle m_{\mu}, m_{\mu} \rangle$ and
$\langle m_{\nu}, m_{\nu} \rangle$. Substituting into
$\lVert m_{\mu} - m_{\nu} \rVert^{2}
 = \langle m_{\mu},m_{\mu}\rangle - 2\langle m_{\mu},m_{\nu}\rangle
 + \langle m_{\nu},m_{\nu}\rangle$ gives the result.
:::

@eq-mmd-expanded is what makes the maximum mean discrepancy practical: it is
written entirely in terms of expectations of the kernel, so it can be estimated
from two samples without any density estimate and without solving the
supremum. The two standard estimators, and the condition on the kernel under
which the maximum mean discrepancy separates distributions at all, are in
@sec-adv-mmd.

This is the discrepancy behind the moment-matching generative models, and it is
where McGAN and MMD-GAN enter in the next lecture.

## Wasserstein distances {#sec-wasserstein}

We now build the second family. Instead of comparing $\mu$ and $\nu$ where they
sit, we ask what it would cost to carry the mass of one onto the other. The
bookkeeping device for "carrying mass" is a joint distribution.

::: {#def-coupling}
## Coupling
Let $\mu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})$ and $\nu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})$.
A coupling of $\mu$ and $\nu$ is a probability measure $\pi$ on
$\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$ whose marginals are $\mu$ and $\nu$:

$$
\pi(A \times \mathcal{Y}) = \mu(A) , \qquad
\pi(\mathcal{X} \times B) = \nu(B)
$$ {#eq-marginals}

for all measurable $A \subseteq \mathcal{X}$, $B \subseteq \mathcal{Y}$. The
set of couplings is written $\Pi(\mu,\nu)$.
:::

Read $\pi(dx,dy)$ as the amount of mass moved from $x$ to $y$. The two
constraints in @eq-marginals say that everything sent out of $x$ adds up to
what $\mu$ had there, and everything arriving at $y$ adds up to what $\nu$
needs there. The set $\Pi(\mu,\nu)$ is never empty: the product measure
$\mu \otimes \nu$, which ignores where mass came from, is always a coupling.

![A coupling and the two marginals it must reproduce. The shaded density is a
joint $\pi$ on the plane; the curve above is its first marginal and the curve
to the right its second, each obtained by integrating out the other
coordinate. @eq-marginals asks exactly that these two curves be $\mu$ and
$\nu$. Nothing asks the joint to be the product of them --- this one is not,
having two modes where a product would have four --- and the freedom left over
is the set $\Pi(\mu,\nu)$ that @def-wasserstein minimises over. From the
course slides.](figures/lec01/slides-joint-marginals.png){#fig-joint-marginals width=55%}


::: {#def-wasserstein}
## Wasserstein distance
Let $(\mathcal{M}, d)$ be a Polish metric space and let $p \geq 1$. For
$\mu, \nu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{M})$ with finite $p$-th moments, the $p$-th
Wasserstein distance is

$$
W_{p}(\mu,\nu) := \left(
  \inf_{\pi \in \Pi(\mu,\nu)}
  \int_{\mathcal{M} \times \mathcal{M}} d(x,y)^{p} \, d\pi(x,y)
\right)^{1/p}
= \left( \inf_{\pi \in \Pi(\mu,\nu)}
  \mathbb{E}_{\pi} \bigl[ d(X,Y)^{p} \bigr] \right)^{1/p} .
$$ {#eq-wasserstein}
:::

For $p = 1$ this is the earth-mover distance: the least total amount of
"mass times distance" needed to rearrange one pile of earth into the other.
The name is worth taking literally, because it is the source of the intuition
that @fig-saturation makes precise --- moving two separated piles closer
together reduces the cost continuously, whereas asking whether they overlap
gives the same answer until the instant they touch.

That @eq-wasserstein really is a metric, and not merely a divergence, is the
structural fact that distinguishes this family from @sec-f-divergences.

::: {#thm-wp-metric}
## Wasserstein is a metric
For $p \geq 1$, $W_{p}$ satisfies all four axioms of @def-metric-axioms on the set of
probability measures on $\mathcal{M}$ with finite $p$-th moments.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Non-negativity* is immediate, since $d^{p} \geq 0$.

*Symmetry.* If $\pi \in \Pi(\mu,\nu)$, let $S(x,y) = (y,x)$ and put
$\pi' = S_{\#}\pi$. By @eq-pushforward its marginals are those of $\pi$ in the
opposite order, so $\pi' \in \Pi(\nu,\mu)$, and by
@lem-change-of-variables its cost is
$\int d(y,x)^{p} d\pi = \int d(x,y)^{p} d\pi$ because $d$ is symmetric. So
$S_{\#}$ is a cost-preserving bijection between $\Pi(\mu,\nu)$ and
$\Pi(\nu,\mu)$, and the two infima agree.

*Identity of indiscernibles.* If $\mu = \nu$, the coupling
$\pi = (\mathrm{id},\mathrm{id})_{\#}\mu$ concentrated on the diagonal has cost
$\int d(x,x)^{p} d\mu = 0$, so $W_{p}(\mu,\mu) = 0$. Conversely suppose
$W_{p}(\mu,\nu) = 0$ and let $\pi$ be an optimal coupling, which exists by
@thm-kantorovich-existence --- this is the one place the proof uses the
standing assumption of @def-wasserstein that $\mathcal{M}$ is Polish, the cost
$d^{p}$ being continuous and hence lower semicontinuous. Then $\int d(x,y)^{p} d\pi = 0$ with a
non-negative integrand, so $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $x = y$ for $\pi$-almost
every pair; that is, $\pi$ is concentrated on the diagonal
$\Delta = \{(x,x)\}$, a measurable set since $\mathcal{M}$ is metric. As
$\pi(\Delta) = 1$, intersecting with $\Delta$ leaves any $\pi$-measure
unchanged, and for measurable $A$ the sets
$(A \times \mathcal{M}) \cap \Delta$ and $(\mathcal{M} \times A) \cap \Delta$
coincide --- both are $\{(x,x) : x \in A\}$. Hence

$$
\mu(A) = \pi(A \times \mathcal{M}) = \pi(\mathcal{M} \times A) = \nu(A) ,
$$

and $\mu = \nu$.

*Triangle inequality.* Let $\mu_{1}, \mu_{2}, \mu_{3}$ be given and take
$\pi_{12} \in \Pi(\mu_{1},\mu_{2})$ and $\pi_{23} \in \Pi(\mu_{2},\mu_{3})$.
The gluing lemma provides a measure $\sigma$ on
$\mathcal{M} \times \mathcal{M} \times \mathcal{M}$ whose projection onto the
first two coordinates is $\pi_{12}$ and onto the last two is $\pi_{23}$; it is
built by disintegrating both couplings over their shared marginal $\mu_{2}$ and
setting
$d\sigma(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})
 = d\pi_{12}(x_{1} \mid x_{2}) \, d\pi_{23}(x_{3} \mid x_{2}) \, d\mu_{2}(x_{2})$.
Its projection onto the first and third coordinates is some
$\pi_{13} \in \Pi(\mu_{1},\mu_{3})$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
  W_{p}(\mu_{1},\mu_{3})
    &\leq \left( \int d(x_{1},x_{3})^{p} \, d\sigma \right)^{1/p} \\
    &\leq \left( \int \bigl( d(x_{1},x_{2}) + d(x_{2},x_{3}) \bigr)^{p}
            d\sigma \right)^{1/p} \\
    &\leq \left( \int d(x_{1},x_{2})^{p} d\sigma \right)^{1/p}
        + \left( \int d(x_{2},x_{3})^{p} d\sigma \right)^{1/p} \\
    &= \left( \int d^{p} \, d\pi_{12} \right)^{1/p}
     + \left( \int d^{p} \, d\pi_{23} \right)^{1/p} ,
\end{aligned}
$$

using the triangle inequality for $d$ in the second step and Minkowski's
inequality in $L^{p}(\sigma)$ in the third. Taking the infimum over
$\pi_{12}$ and $\pi_{23}$ separately gives
$W_{p}(\mu_{1},\mu_{3}) \leq W_{p}(\mu_{1},\mu_{2}) + W_{p}(\mu_{2},\mu_{3})$.
:::

By Jensen's inequality $W_{1} \leq W_{p}$ for $p \geq 1$, so the Wasserstein
distances form an increasing family. We will use $W_{1}$ almost exclusively,
because it is the one with a dual formulation simple enough to implement.
Being a metric is not by itself what matters for @sec-synthesis --- *which*
topology the metric induces is --- and @sec-adv-topology settles that.

## Monge's formulation {#sec-monge}

Historically the transport problem was posed not with couplings but with maps:
each grain of earth is assigned one destination.

::: {#def-transport-map}
## Transportation map
A measurable $T : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}$ transports
$\mu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})$ to $\nu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})$ if

$$
\nu(B) = \mu\bigl( T^{-1}(B) \bigr)
\quad \text{for all measurable } B ,
$$ {#eq-transport-constraint}

that is, if $\nu = T_{\#}\mu$ in the sense of @def-pushforward.
:::

::: {#def-monge}
## Monge's problem
Given a cost $c : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y} \to [0,\infty]$, Monge's
optimal transport problem is

$$
\min_{T} \; \mathbb{M}(T)
  := \int_{\mathcal{X}} c\bigl( x, T(x) \bigr) \, d\mu(x)
\qquad \text{subject to} \quad \nu = T_{\#}\mu .
$$ {#eq-monge}
:::

The objective is benign; the constraint is not. The map $T \mapsto T_{\#}\mu$
is nonlinear, and the feasible set $\{ T : T_{\#}\mu = \nu \}$ is not convex:
if $T_{0}$ and $T_{1}$ both push $\mu$ to $\nu$, there is no reason for
$\tfrac{1}{2}(T_{0}+T_{1})$ to do so. So @eq-monge cannot be attacked by the
standard machinery of convex optimisation. Worse, it can be infeasible.

::: {#prp-monge-fails}
## Monge's problem may admit no solution
Let $\mu = \delta_{0}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and
$\nu = \tfrac{1}{2}(\delta_{-1} + \delta_{1})$. Then no measurable $T$
satisfies $T_{\#}\mu = \nu$, so @eq-monge has no feasible point at all.
:::

::: {.proof}
Suppose $T_{\#}\mu = \nu$. For any measurable $B$, @eq-transport-constraint
gives $\nu(B) = \mu(T^{-1}(B)) = \delta_{0}(T^{-1}(B))$, which is $1$ if
$0 \in T^{-1}(B)$ and $0$ otherwise. So $\nu(B) \in \{0,1\}$ for every $B$. But
$\nu(\{1\}) = \tfrac{1}{2}$, a contradiction.
:::

The obstruction is plain once seen: a map sends the single atom at $0$
somewhere, and it can only send it to one place, whereas $\nu$ requires the
mass to end up in two. A map cannot split mass. This is exactly what
@sec-kantorovich repairs. Atoms are the crudest obstruction but not the
only one; @sec-adv-monge gives two more, one of which shows that a non-atomic
$\mu$ does not make Monge's problem well behaved either.


When a solution does exist, the one-dimensional case can be written down.

::: {#thm-monge-1d}
## Transport on the line
Let $\mu, \nu$ be probability measures on $\mathbb{R}$ with continuous, strictly
increasing distribution functions $F$ and $G$. Then
$T = G^{-1} \circ F$ satisfies $T_{\#}\mu = \nu$, and for
$c(x,y) = \lvert x - y \rvert^{p}$ with $p \geq 1$ it is optimal, giving

$$
W_{p}(\mu,\nu)
  = \left( \int_{0}^{1}
      \bigl\lvert F^{-1}(z) - G^{-1}(z) \bigr\rvert^{p} dz
    \right)^{1/p}
  = \left( \int_{\mathbb{R}}
      \bigl\lvert x - G^{-1}(F(x)) \bigr\rvert^{p} dF(x)
    \right)^{1/p} .
$$ {#eq-w-1d}
:::

::: {.proof}
We prove the push-forward claim and the formula; optimality of the monotone
map for convex costs is classical and we cite it rather than reprove it.

Fix $y \in \mathbb{R}$. Since $G$ is continuous and strictly increasing, and
likewise $F$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
  (T_{\#}\mu)\bigl( (-\infty, y] \bigr)
    &= \mu\bigl( \{ x : G^{-1}(F(x)) \leq y \} \bigr) \\
    &= \mu\bigl( \{ x : F(x) \leq G(y) \} \bigr) \\
    &= \mu\bigl( \{ x : x \leq F^{-1}(G(y)) \} \bigr) \\
    &= F\bigl( F^{-1}(G(y)) \bigr) = G(y) ,
\end{aligned}
$$

where the second and third lines apply the increasing bijections $G$ and
$F^{-1}$ to both sides of the inequality. So $T_{\#}\mu$ and $\nu$ have the
same distribution function, hence are equal.

Given optimality, the cost of $T$ is $W_{p}^{p}$. By
@lem-change-of-variables with the substitution $x = F^{-1}(z)$, which carries
Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$ to $\mu$,

$$
\int_{\mathbb{R}} \lvert x - T(x) \rvert^{p} \, d\mu(x)
  = \int_{0}^{1} \bigl\lvert F^{-1}(z) - G^{-1}(F(F^{-1}(z))) \bigr\rvert^{p} dz
  = \int_{0}^{1} \bigl\lvert F^{-1}(z) - G^{-1}(z) \bigr\rvert^{p} dz ,
$$

which is @eq-w-1d.
:::

![Transport on the line. The map $T = G^{-1} \circ F$ carries the quantile of
$\mu$ at level $z$ to the quantile of $\nu$ at the same level, so the
horizontal gap between the two inverse distribution functions is exactly the
distance each unit of mass travels. Integrating the $p$-th power of that gap
over $z$ gives @eq-w-1d.](figures/lec01/jungwoo-ahn-fig7.png){#fig-quantile width=85%}

In @fig-quantile the map is read off horizontally: fix a level $z$, find the
point that $\mu$ places at that quantile and the point that $\nu$ places at the
same quantile, and the arrow between them is where that parcel of mass goes.
The next example carries this through with numbers.

::: {#exm-uniform}
## A transport computed by hand
Let $\mu = \mathrm{Uniform}[0,1]$ and $\nu = \mathrm{Uniform}[2,4]$. Then
$F(x) = x$ on $[0,1]$ and $G(y) = (y-2)/2$ on $[2,4]$, so
$F^{-1}(z) = z$ and $G^{-1}(z) = 2 + 2z$, and the optimal map is

$$
T(x) = G^{-1}(F(x)) = 2 + 2x .
$$

The map stretches the unit interval to twice its length and shifts it. By
@eq-w-1d the transport costs are

$$
W_{1} = \int_{0}^{1} \lvert z - (2+2z) \rvert \, dz
      = \int_{0}^{1} (2 + z) \, dz = \frac{5}{2} ,
$$

$$
W_{2} = \left( \int_{0}^{1} (2+z)^{2} \, dz \right)^{1/2}
      = \left( \frac{(2+z)^{3}}{3} \Big\vert_{0}^{1} \right)^{1/2}
      = \left( \frac{27 - 8}{3} \right)^{1/2}
      = \sqrt{\frac{19}{3}} \approx 2.5166 .
$$

Two sanity checks. The value $W_{1} = 5/2$ equals the distance between the two
means, $3 - 1/2$, as it must here because $T(x) - x = 2 + x$ never changes
sign, so no mass moves against the flow. And $W_{1} \leq W_{2}$, as Jensen's
inequality requires.
:::

The computation is short enough to check numerically, which is worth doing once
to see that the coupling really is optimal and not merely feasible:

```{.python}
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import wasserstein_distance

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.uniform(0.0, 1.0, 2_000_000)      # mu  = Uniform[0, 1]
y = rng.uniform(2.0, 4.0, 2_000_000)      # nu  = Uniform[2, 4]

print(wasserstein_distance(x, y))         # ~2.5000   matches W_1 = 5/2
print(np.mean(np.abs(x - (2 + 2 * x))))   # ~2.5000   cost of T(x) = 2 + 2x
print(np.sqrt(np.mean((x - (2 + 2 * x)) ** 2)))   # ~2.5166  matches W_2
```

A second instance, with a map that is not affine, shows the two readings of
@thm-monge-1d side by side.

![One transport problem, seen twice. **A.** The push-forward of
@eq-pushforward made concrete: $T(x) = \sqrt{x}$ carries
$X \sim \mathrm{Uniform}[0,1]$ to the law with density $2y$ on $[0,1]$, and
the target event $[\tfrac{1}{2}, 1]$ receives exactly the mass its preimage
$[\tfrac{1}{4}, 1]$ had, namely $\tfrac{3}{4}$. This $T$ is the monotone map
$G^{-1} \circ F$ of @thm-monge-1d, since $F(x) = x$ and $G(y) = y^{2}$.
**B.** The same pair through their quantile functions. @eq-w-1d integrates the
horizontal gap between $F^{-1}$ and $G^{-1}$, so $W_{1}$ is the shaded area
between the two curves, here
$\int_{0}^{1} (\sqrt{u} - u) \, du = \tfrac{2}{3} - \tfrac{1}{2} =
\tfrac{1}{6}$.](figures/lec01/jun-brro-transport-overview.png){#fig-transport-overview width=95%}

## Kantorovich's relaxation {#sec-kantorovich}

Kantorovich's reformulation replaces the map by a coupling, and so allows mass
at a single point to be split between several destinations. It is the problem
we already wrote down as @eq-wasserstein, now stated for a general cost.

::: {#def-kantorovich}
## Kantorovich's problem
Given $\mu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})$, $\nu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})$ and
a cost $c$,

$$
\mathbb{K}(\pi) := \int_{\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}} c(x,y) \, d\pi(x,y) ,
\qquad
\min_{\pi \in \Pi(\mu,\nu)} \mathbb{K}(\pi) .
$$ {#eq-kantorovich}
:::

Three things improve at once. The objective is linear in $\pi$, the
constraint set $\Pi(\mu,\nu)$ is convex --- a convex combination of couplings
is a coupling, since @eq-marginals is linear in $\pi$ --- and on finite spaces
the whole thing is a linear program, the observation for which Kantorovich
shared the 1975 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics. @sec-adv-lp writes that
program out, and reads off it both why the dual of @sec-duality is the
practical formulation and when the relaxation costs nothing.


::: {#prp-monge-ge-kantorovich}
## The relaxation is genuine
Every transport map induces a coupling of the same cost, so

$$
\min_{\pi \in \Pi(\mu,\nu)} \mathbb{K}(\pi)
  \; \leq \; \inf_{T : T_{\#}\mu = \nu} \mathbb{M}(T) .
$$ {#eq-relaxation}
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $T$ satisfy $T_{\#}\mu = \nu$ and put
$\pi_{T} = (\mathrm{id}, T)_{\#} \mu$, the law of $(X, T(X))$ for
$X \sim \mu$. Its first marginal is $\mu$ because the first coordinate of
$(\mathrm{id},T)$ is the identity, and its second marginal is $T_{\#}\mu = \nu$;
so $\pi_{T} \in \Pi(\mu,\nu)$. By @lem-change-of-variables its cost is

$$
\int c(x,y) \, d\pi_{T}(x,y) = \int c\bigl( x, T(x) \bigr) \, d\mu(x)
  = \mathbb{M}(T) .
$$

Hence every value attained by $\mathbb{M}$ is attained by $\mathbb{K}$, and the
infimum over the larger set is no larger.
:::

The inequality in @eq-relaxation can be strict, and @prp-monge-fails is the
extreme case: the right-hand side is an infimum over the empty set, hence
$+\infty$, while the left-hand side is finite. Indeed with $\mu = \delta_{0}$,
$\nu = \tfrac{1}{2}(\delta_{-1}+\delta_{1})$ and $c(x,y) = \lvert x-y \rvert$,
the only coupling is
$\pi = \tfrac{1}{2}\delta_{(0,-1)} + \tfrac{1}{2}\delta_{(0,1)}$ --- it splits
the atom, which no map can do --- and its cost is $1$. @fig-monge-kantorovich
draws the two formulations on this example.

![Monge versus Kantorovich. On the left a transport map must send all the mass
at a source point to a single destination, which is impossible when the source
is one atom and the target is two. On the right a coupling may split that atom,
and the resulting transport plan is feasible and
optimal.](figures/lec01/jungwoo-ahn-fig6.png){#fig-monge-kantorovich width=85%}

Unlike Monge's problem, Kantorovich's always has a solution.

::: {#thm-kantorovich-existence}
## Existence of an optimal coupling
Let $\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}$ be Polish spaces, $\mu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})$,
$\nu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})$, and let
$c : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y} \to [0,\infty]$ be lower semicontinuous.
Then the minimum in @eq-kantorovich is attained.
:::

::: {.proof}
The set $\Pi(\mu,\nu)$ is non-empty, since $\mu \otimes \nu$ lies in it.

*It is tight.* Let $\varepsilon > 0$. By Ulam's theorem, Borel probability
measures on a Polish space are tight, so there are compact sets
$K_{1} \subseteq \mathcal{X}$ and $K_{2} \subseteq \mathcal{Y}$ with
$\mu(K_{1}^{c}) \leq \varepsilon/2$ and $\nu(K_{2}^{c}) \leq \varepsilon/2$.
For any $\pi \in \Pi(\mu,\nu)$, the complement of the compact set
$K_{1} \times K_{2}$ is contained in
$(K_{1}^{c} \times \mathcal{Y}) \cup (\mathcal{X} \times K_{2}^{c})$, so by
@eq-marginals

$$
\pi\bigl( (K_{1} \times K_{2})^{c} \bigr)
  \leq \mu(K_{1}^{c}) + \nu(K_{2}^{c}) \leq \varepsilon .
$$

The bound is uniform over $\Pi(\mu,\nu)$, so the family is tight and, by
Prokhorov's theorem, relatively compact for the weak topology.

*It is closed.* If $\pi_{n} \to \pi$ weakly with $\pi_{n} \in \Pi(\mu,\nu)$,
then for bounded continuous $h$ on $\mathcal{X}$, the function
$(x,y) \mapsto h(x)$ is bounded and continuous on the product, so
$\int h(x) d\pi = \lim \int h(x) d\pi_{n} = \int h \, d\mu$. Hence the first
marginal of $\pi$ is $\mu$, and symmetrically the second is $\nu$. So
$\Pi(\mu,\nu)$ is weakly closed, and with the previous paragraph, weakly
compact.

*The objective is lower semicontinuous.* A non-negative lower semicontinuous
$c$ is the pointwise increasing limit of bounded continuous functions
$c_{k}$. For each $k$, $\pi \mapsto \int c_{k} \, d\pi$ is weakly continuous,
and a supremum of continuous functions is lower semicontinuous, so
$\pi \mapsto \int c \, d\pi = \sup_{k} \int c_{k} \, d\pi$ is lower
semicontinuous.

A lower semicontinuous function on a non-empty compact set attains its infimum,
which is the claim.
:::

## Kantorovich duality {#sec-duality}

@eq-kantorovich is a linear program over an infinite-dimensional convex set, so
it has a dual. The dual turns out to be the formulation that generative models
actually implement, because it needs only the two marginals and never the joint
measure.

::: {#thm-kantorovich-duality}
## Kantorovich duality
Let $\mu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})$, $\nu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})$ with
$\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}$ Polish, and let
$c : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y} \to [0,+\infty]$ be lower semicontinuous.
Define

$$
\mathbb{J}(\varphi,\psi)
  = \int_{\mathcal{X}} \varphi \, d\mu + \int_{\mathcal{Y}} \psi \, d\nu ,
\qquad
\Phi_{c} = \bigl\{ (\varphi,\psi) \in L^{1}(\mu) \times L^{1}(\nu) :
  \varphi(x) + \psi(y) \leq c(x,y) \bigr\} ,
$$ {#eq-dual-objective}

the inequality holding for $\mu$-almost every $x$ and $\nu$-almost every $y$.
Then

$$
\min_{\pi \in \Pi(\mu,\nu)} \mathbb{K}(\pi)
  = \sup_{(\varphi,\psi) \in \Phi_{c}} \mathbb{J}(\varphi,\psi) .
$$ {#eq-ot-duality}
:::

::: {.proof}
*Weak duality, in general.* Let $\pi \in \Pi(\mu,\nu)$ and
$(\varphi,\psi) \in \Phi_{c}$. Because the marginals of $\pi$ are $\mu$ and
$\nu$, integrating a function of $x$ alone against $\pi$ is the same as
integrating it against $\mu$, and likewise for $y$ and $\nu$. Hence

$$
\mathbb{J}(\varphi,\psi)
  = \int \varphi(x) \, d\pi + \int \psi(y) \, d\pi
  = \int \bigl( \varphi(x) + \psi(y) \bigr) d\pi
  \leq \int c(x,y) \, d\pi
  = \mathbb{K}(\pi) ,
$$

the inequality being the constraint defining $\Phi_{c}$ integrated against the
non-negative measure $\pi$. Taking the supremum on the left and the infimum on
the right gives $\sup \mathbb{J} \leq \min \mathbb{K}$.

*Strong duality, on finite spaces.* Let
$\mathcal{X} = \{x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\}$ and
$\mathcal{Y} = \{y_{1},\dots,y_{n}\}$, write $\mu_{i}, \nu_{j}, c_{ij}$ and
$\pi_{ij}$. The problem is the linear program

$$
\min_{\pi \geq 0} \; \sum_{i,j} c_{ij}\pi_{ij}
\quad \text{subject to} \quad
\sum_{j} \pi_{ij} = \mu_{i} , \quad \sum_{i} \pi_{ij} = \nu_{j} .
$$

Attach multipliers $\varphi_{i}$ and $\psi_{j}$ to the two families of
constraints. The Lagrangian is

$$
\begin{aligned}
  L(\pi,\varphi,\psi)
    &= \sum_{i,j} c_{ij}\pi_{ij}
     + \sum_{i} \varphi_{i}\Bigl( \mu_{i} - \sum_{j}\pi_{ij} \Bigr)
     + \sum_{j} \psi_{j}\Bigl( \nu_{j} - \sum_{i}\pi_{ij} \Bigr) \\
    &= \sum_{i,j} \pi_{ij}\bigl( c_{ij} - \varphi_{i} - \psi_{j} \bigr)
     + \sum_{i} \varphi_{i}\mu_{i} + \sum_{j} \psi_{j}\nu_{j} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Minimising over $\pi \geq 0$ sends the first sum to $-\infty$ unless every
coefficient is non-negative, and gives $0$ when they all are. So the dual
function is finite exactly on $\{ \varphi_{i} + \psi_{j} \leq c_{ij} \}$, where
it equals $\mathbb{J}(\varphi,\psi)$, and the dual problem is
$\sup_{\Phi_{c}} \mathbb{J}$. The primal is feasible, since $\mu \otimes \nu$
is a coupling, and bounded below by $0$, so linear programming duality gives
equality of the two optimal values. The passage from finite spaces to Polish
spaces is by approximation and is given in Villani, Theorem 1.3.
:::

The dual constraint couples $\varphi$ and $\psi$, but only in one direction:
for a fixed $\varphi$ there is a best possible $\psi$, and it can be written
down.

::: {#def-c-transform}
## c-transform and c-concavity
For $\varphi : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ and
$\psi : \mathcal{Y} \to \mathbb{R}$, the $c$-transforms are

$$
\varphi^{c}(y) := \inf_{x} \bigl\{ c(x,y) - \varphi(x) \bigr\} ,
\qquad
\psi^{c}(x) := \inf_{y} \bigl\{ c(x,y) - \psi(y) \bigr\} .
$$ {#eq-c-transform}

A function $\varphi$ is called $c$-concave if $\varphi = \psi^{c}$ for some
$\psi$. Optimal $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are called Kantorovich potentials.
:::

::: {#prp-dual-reduction}
## The dual is a supremum over one potential
The dual problem in @eq-ot-duality can be written

$$
\sup_{(\varphi,\psi) \in \Phi_{c}} \mathbb{J}(\varphi,\psi)
  = \sup_{\varphi} \left\{
      \int_{\mathcal{X}} \varphi \, d\mu
      + \int_{\mathcal{Y}} \varphi^{c} \, d\nu \right\}
  = \sup_{\psi} \left\{
      \int_{\mathcal{X}} \psi^{c} \, d\mu
      + \int_{\mathcal{Y}} \psi \, d\nu \right\} ,
$$ {#eq-dual-reduced}

and the supremum may be restricted to $c$-concave $\varphi$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Fix $\varphi$. The constraint $(\varphi,\psi) \in \Phi_{c}$ says
$\psi(y) \leq c(x,y) - \varphi(x)$ for every $x$, which is exactly
$\psi(y) \leq \varphi^{c}(y)$ by @eq-c-transform. Since $\mathbb{J}$ is
increasing in $\psi$ and $\nu \geq 0$, the largest admissible choice
$\psi = \varphi^{c}$ is optimal. This gives the first equality in
@eq-dual-reduced, and the second follows by the symmetric argument with the
roles of the two potentials exchanged.

For the restriction, apply the transform twice. For every $x$ and $y$,
$\varphi^{c}(y) \leq c(x,y) - \varphi(x)$, so
$c(x,y) - \varphi^{c}(y) \geq \varphi(x)$; taking the infimum over $y$ gives

$$
\varphi^{cc}(x) = \inf_{y} \bigl\{ c(x,y) - \varphi^{c}(y) \bigr\}
  \geq \varphi(x) .
$$

So replacing $\varphi$ by $\varphi^{cc}$ never decreases
$\int \varphi \, d\mu$. Applying the same inequality to $\varphi^{c}$ gives
$\varphi^{ccc} \geq \varphi^{c}$, while $\varphi^{cc} \geq \varphi$ and the
order-reversing nature of the transform give $\varphi^{ccc} \leq \varphi^{c}$;
hence $\varphi^{ccc} = \varphi^{c}$ and the second term is unchanged. So
$(\varphi^{cc}, \varphi^{c})$ is admissible, has objective value at least that
of $(\varphi, \varphi^{c})$, and $\varphi^{cc}$ is $c$-concave by construction.
:::

### The Kantorovich--Rubinstein form of the Wasserstein-1 distance

Everything above holds for a general cost. For the particular cost
$c(x,y) = \lVert x - y \rVert$ the $c$-transform collapses, and the dual takes
the form that W-GAN implements.

::: {#lem-ctransform-lipschitz}
## The c-transform of a 1-Lipschitz function
Let $c(x,y) = \lVert x-y \rVert$ and let
$\varphi \in \mathrm{Lip}_{1}(\mathcal{X})$. Then $\varphi^{c} = -\varphi$.
Moreover a function is $c$-concave for this cost if and only if it is
$1$-Lipschitz, so the two classes coincide.
:::

::: {.proof}
From @eq-c-transform, choosing the particular point $x = y$ in the infimum,

$$
\varphi^{c}(y) = \inf_{x} \bigl\{ \lVert x-y \rVert - \varphi(x) \bigr\}
  \leq \lVert y-y \rVert - \varphi(y) = -\varphi(y) .
$$

In the other direction, the $1$-Lipschitz property gives
$\varphi(x) \leq \varphi(y) + \lVert x-y \rVert$ for every $x$, hence
$\lVert x-y \rVert - \varphi(x) \geq -\varphi(y)$ for every $x$, and taking
the infimum over $x$,

$$
\varphi^{c}(y) \geq -\varphi(y) .
$$

The two inequalities give $\varphi^{c} = -\varphi$.

For the second claim, a $c$-concave function is by definition
$\psi^{c}(x) = \inf_{y}\{\lVert x-y \rVert - \psi(y)\}$, an infimum of
functions of $x$ each of which is $1$-Lipschitz; an infimum of a family of
$1$-Lipschitz functions is $1$-Lipschitz wherever it is finite. Conversely a
$1$-Lipschitz $\varphi$ is $c$-concave: taking $\psi = -\varphi$,

$$
\psi^{c}(x) = \inf_{y} \bigl\{ \lVert x-y \rVert + \varphi(y) \bigr\}
  = \varphi(x) ,
$$

because $\varphi(y) \geq \varphi(x) - \lVert x-y \rVert$ makes every term at
least $\varphi(x)$, with equality at $y = x$. So the two classes coincide.
:::

::: {#thm-kantorovich-rubinstein}
## Kantorovich--Rubinstein
For $c(x,y) = \lVert x-y \rVert$,

$$
W_{1}(\mu,\nu)
  = \min_{\pi \in \Pi(\mu,\nu)}
      \int \lVert x-y \rVert \, d\pi(x,y)
  = \sup_{\varphi \in \mathrm{Lip}_{1}(\mathcal{X})}
      \left\{ \int_{\mathcal{X}} \varphi \, d\mu
            - \int_{\mathcal{X}} \varphi \, d\nu \right\} .
$$ {#eq-kr}
:::

::: {.proof}
The first equality is @def-wasserstein with $p = 1$ and $d(x,y) =
\lVert x-y \rVert$. For the second, start from @eq-dual-reduced, whose
supremum may be taken over $c$-concave $\varphi$ only. By
@lem-ctransform-lipschitz the $c$-concave functions for this cost are exactly
the $1$-Lipschitz ones, and on that class $\varphi^{c} = -\varphi$.
Substituting,

$$
\sup_{\varphi} \left\{ \int \varphi \, d\mu + \int \varphi^{c} \, d\nu \right\}
  = \sup_{\varphi \in \mathrm{Lip}_{1}}
    \left\{ \int \varphi \, d\mu - \int \varphi \, d\nu \right\} ,
$$

and @thm-kantorovich-duality equates this with the primal minimum.
:::

Compare @eq-kr with @def-ipm. The right-hand side is exactly the integral
probability metric $d_{\mathcal{F}}$ with
$\mathcal{F} = \mathrm{Lip}_{1}(\mathcal{X})$ --- the case promised in
@sec-ipm and left unproved there. One step is needed to match the two
expressions, since @def-ipm carries an absolute value and @eq-kr does not, and
it is the symmetry assumed in @sec-ipm: $\mathrm{Lip}_{1}$ is closed under
$\varphi \mapsto -\varphi$, so the supremum of the signed difference already
equals the supremum of its absolute value.

The two families of statistical distance
introduced in this chapter, one built from density ratios and one built from
transport cost, meet at this single identity: $W_{1}$ is simultaneously the
cheapest way to move mass and the most a $1$-Lipschitz test function can tell
the two distributions apart.

The practical consequence is the one the lecture stresses. The primal in
@eq-kr requires optimising over joint measures on
$\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X}$, which is hopeless in high dimension. The dual
requires only a single function $\varphi$ and two expectations, each estimated
from a sample of the corresponding marginal. Parameterise $\varphi$ by a
network constrained to be $1$-Lipschitz, maximise the bracket in @eq-kr, and
the result estimates $W_{1}$; that network is the W-GAN critic, and the
Lipschitz constraint is why it is clipped or gradient-penalised rather than
left free.

## Brenier's theorem and the Gaussian case {#sec-brenier}

Kantorovich's relaxation buys existence at the price of abandoning maps. For
the quadratic cost the map comes back, and with a great deal of extra
structure.

::: {#thm-brenier}
## Brenier
Let $c(x,y) = \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert x-y \rVert^{2}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, and let
$\mu, \nu$ have finite second moments with $\mu$ absolutely continuous with
respect to Lebesgue measure. Then the optimal coupling of @eq-kantorovich is
unique and is induced by a map: there is a convex function $u$ such that
$T = \nabla u$ satisfies $T_{\#}\mu = \nu$ and
$\pi = (\mathrm{id}, T)_{\#}\mu$ is optimal. The map $T$ is unique
$\mu$-almost everywhere.
:::

::: {.proof}
Expand the cost as
$c(x,y) = \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert x \rVert^{2} - \langle x,y \rangle
 + \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert y \rVert^{2}$ and change variables in the dual, setting

$$
u(x) = \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert x \rVert^{2} - \varphi(x) ,
\qquad
v(y) = \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert y \rVert^{2} - \psi(y) .
$$

The dual constraint $\varphi(x) + \psi(y) \leq c(x,y)$ becomes, after
substituting and cancelling the two quadratic terms,

$$
\langle x, y \rangle \leq u(x) + v(y) ,
$$ {#eq-fenchel-young}

which is precisely the Fenchel--Young inequality for the pair $u, v$. In
these variables the $c$-transform of @def-c-transform is the Legendre
transform, the relation $\psi = \varphi^{c}$ reading $v = u^{\ast}$; this is
worked out in @sec-adv-legendre. By @prp-dual-reduction the supremum may be
restricted to $c$-concave $\varphi$, which says here that $u$ may be taken
convex and lower semicontinuous with $u = v^{\ast}$.

Let $\pi$ be an optimal coupling and $(\varphi,\psi)$ optimal potentials, which
exist for this cost because $\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert x-y \rVert^{2} \leq
\lVert x \rVert^{2} + \lVert y \rVert^{2}$ and both measures have finite second
moments; @sec-adv-duality states the hypothesis in general. Weak duality was an
integrated inequality, and equality of the two optimal values forces the
non-negative integrand $c - \varphi - \psi$ to vanish $\pi$-almost everywhere.
So @eq-fenchel-young holds with equality for $\pi$-almost every $(x,y)$:

$$
\langle x,y \rangle = u(x) + v(y) .
$$

The case of equality in the Fenchel--Young inequality is exactly
$y \in \partial u(x)$.

Next we check that $u$ is finite and differentiable where the argument needs
it. This deserves a step rather than an appeal: $u = v^{\ast}$ is a supremum of
affine functions and may perfectly well be $+\infty$ off its effective domain.
The equality above holds on a set of full $\pi$-measure, whose projection to
the first coordinate therefore has full $\mu$-measure, and on it
$u(x) = \langle x,y \rangle - v(y)$ is finite. A convex function finite at each
point of a set is finite on that set's convex hull, so $\mathrm{dom}\,u$
contains the convex hull $K$ of a set of full $\mu$-measure. Since
$\mu \ll \mathrm{Lebesgue}$ cannot charge a hyperplane, $K$ has non-empty
interior; and the boundary of a convex set in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is
Lebesgue-null, so $\mu(\partial K) = 0$ and $\mu$-almost every $x$ lies in
$\mathrm{int}\,K \subseteq \mathrm{int}\,\mathrm{dom}\,u$. On the interior of
its domain a finite convex function is locally Lipschitz, hence differentiable
outside a set of Lebesgue measure zero by Rademacher's theorem; that
exceptional set is $\mu$-null too. So for $\mu$-almost every $x$ the
subdifferential is a single point, $\partial u(x) = \{\nabla u(x)\}$.
Therefore $y = \nabla u(x)$ for $\pi$-almost every $(x,y)$, which says $\pi$ is
concentrated on the graph of $T = \nabla u$ and hence
$\pi = (\mathrm{id},T)_{\#}\mu$. Its second marginal is $T_{\#}\mu$ and must
equal $\nu$.

*Uniqueness.* Everything above applies to *any* optimal coupling, so each one
is concentrated on the graph of the gradient of some convex potential. Let
$\pi$ and $\pi'$ be optimal, carried by the graphs of $T$ and $T'$. The
objective @eq-kantorovich is linear and $\Pi(\mu,\nu)$ convex, so
$\tfrac{1}{2}(\pi + \pi')$ is optimal as well, hence also carried by a graph;
a measure carried by a graph assigns to $\mu$-almost every $x$ a single $y$,
which forces $T = T'$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. That gives uniqueness of both
the map and the plan. Note what is *not* being claimed: the potential $u$
itself is pinned down only up to an additive constant on each connected
component of the interior of its domain, so on a disconnected support one may
shift the components independently without changing anything. It is
$\nabla u$, not $u$, that is unique.
:::

The factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$ in the cost is only a normalisation. Multiplying
$c$ by a positive constant rescales the optimal value but leaves the minimising
coupling unchanged, so the map of @thm-brenier is equally optimal for
$c(x,y) = \lVert x-y \rVert^{2}$, which is the cost @def-wasserstein uses at
$p = 2$; the distance computed below is for that unhalved cost.

The theorem says something striking: the optimal transport map for the
quadratic cost is never arbitrary. It is always the gradient of a convex
potential, so it is a curl-free, monotone rearrangement of space. The lecture's
Gaussian formula is the simplest instance where the potential can be written in
closed form.

::: {#prp-gaussian-ot}
## Optimal transport between Gaussians
Let $\mu = \mathcal{N}(m_{U}, \Sigma_{U})$ and
$\nu = \mathcal{N}(m_{V}, \Sigma_{V})$ with $\Sigma_{U}$ positive definite.
Put

$$
A = \Sigma_{U}^{-1/2}
    \bigl( \Sigma_{U}^{1/2} \Sigma_{V} \Sigma_{U}^{1/2} \bigr)^{1/2}
    \Sigma_{U}^{-1/2} ,
\qquad
T_{\mu \to \nu}(u) = m_{V} + A \, (u - m_{U}) .
$$ {#eq-gaussian-map}

Then $A$ is symmetric positive semi-definite, $T_{\mu \to \nu}$ is the gradient
of a convex function, $T_{\mu \to \nu \#}\mu = \nu$, and

$$
W_{2}^{2}(\mu,\nu)
  = \lVert m_{U} - m_{V} \rVert^{2}
  + \operatorname{tr}\Bigl( \Sigma_{U} + \Sigma_{V}
      - 2 \bigl( \Sigma_{U}^{1/2}\Sigma_{V}\Sigma_{U}^{1/2} \bigr)^{1/2}
    \Bigr) .
$$ {#eq-bures}
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $S = \Sigma_{U}^{1/2}$, symmetric positive definite, and
$M = (S \Sigma_{V} S)^{1/2}$, symmetric positive semi-definite, so that
$A = S^{-1} M S^{-1}$.

*Symmetry and positivity.* $A^{\top} = (S^{-1})^{\top} M^{\top} (S^{-1})^{\top}
= S^{-1} M S^{-1} = A$, and for any $z$,
$z^{\top} A z = (S^{-1}z)^{\top} M (S^{-1}z) \geq 0$.

*Gradient of a convex function.* Set
$\phi(u) = \tfrac{1}{2} u^{\top} A u + (m_{V} - A m_{U})^{\top} u$. Then
$\nabla \phi(u) = A u + m_{V} - A m_{U} = T_{\mu \to \nu}(u)$, and $\phi$ is
convex because $A$ is positive semi-definite. By @thm-brenier this identifies
$T_{\mu \to \nu}$ as the optimal map, provided it pushes $\mu$ to $\nu$.

*Push-forward.* If $u \sim \mathcal{N}(m_{U}, \Sigma_{U})$ then
$T_{\mu \to \nu}(u)$ is Gaussian with mean $m_{V}$ and covariance
$A \Sigma_{U} A$. Compute, using $\Sigma_{U} = S^{2}$ and $M^{2} = S\Sigma_{V}S$:

$$
A \Sigma_{U} A
  = S^{-1} M S^{-1} \cdot S^{2} \cdot S^{-1} M S^{-1}
  = S^{-1} M^{2} S^{-1}
  = S^{-1} S \Sigma_{V} S S^{-1}
  = \Sigma_{V} .
$$

So the push-forward is $\mathcal{N}(m_{V},\Sigma_{V}) = \nu$.

*The distance.* By @prp-monge-ge-kantorovich and @thm-brenier the optimal cost
is attained at this map, so with $u \sim \mu$ and
$w = u - m_{U}$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
  W_{2}^{2}(\mu,\nu)
    &= \mathbb{E} \bigl\lVert u - T_{\mu \to \nu}(u) \bigr\rVert^{2}
     = \mathbb{E} \bigl\lVert (m_{U} - m_{V}) + (I - A) w \bigr\rVert^{2} \\
    &= \lVert m_{U} - m_{V} \rVert^{2}
     + \operatorname{tr}\bigl( (I-A) \Sigma_{U} (I-A) \bigr) ,
\end{aligned}
$$

the cross term vanishing because $\mathbb{E}w = 0$. Expanding the trace,

$$
\operatorname{tr}\bigl( \Sigma_{U} - 2 A \Sigma_{U} + A \Sigma_{U} A \bigr)
  = \operatorname{tr}\Sigma_{U} - 2 \operatorname{tr}(A\Sigma_{U})
  + \operatorname{tr}\Sigma_{V} ,
$$

using $A\Sigma_{U}A = \Sigma_{V}$ from above and the symmetry of $A$ and
$\Sigma_{U}$. Finally, by cyclicity of the trace,
$\operatorname{tr}(A\Sigma_{U}) = \operatorname{tr}(S^{-1}MS^{-1}S^{2})
= \operatorname{tr}(S^{-1}MS) = \operatorname{tr}(M)$, which is
$\operatorname{tr}((\Sigma_{U}^{1/2}\Sigma_{V}\Sigma_{U}^{1/2})^{1/2})$.
Substituting gives @eq-bures.
:::

::: {#exm-adain}
## The isotropic case is adaptive instance normalisation
Suppose the two Gaussians are isotropic,
$\Sigma_{U} = \sigma(u)^{2} I$ and $\Sigma_{V} = \sigma(v)^{2} I$. Then
$S = \sigma(u) I$, $M = (\sigma(u)^{2}\sigma(v)^{2} I)^{1/2}
= \sigma(u)\sigma(v) I$, and

$$
A = \frac{1}{\sigma(u)} \cdot \sigma(u)\sigma(v) \cdot \frac{1}{\sigma(u)} I
  = \frac{\sigma(v)}{\sigma(u)} I ,
$$

so @eq-gaussian-map becomes

$$
T_{\mu \to \nu}(u)
  = \mu(v) \mathbf{1} + \frac{\sigma(v)}{\sigma(u)}
    \bigl( u - \mu(u) \mathbf{1} \bigr) ,
$$ {#eq-adain}

writing $\mu(\cdot)$ and $\sigma(\cdot)$ for the scalar mean and standard
deviation. @eq-adain is exactly the adaptive instance normalisation layer used
in style transfer: standardise the content features and rescale them by the
statistics of the style features. So AdaIN is not a heuristic --- it is the
optimal transport map between two isotropic Gaussians, and it will reappear
under that name in the lecture on StyleGAN.
:::

The Gaussian formulas are easy to get wrong by a transpose, so they are worth
checking once numerically:

```{.python}
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import sqrtm

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d = 4
def rand_cov():
    B = rng.normal(size=(d, d))
    return B @ B.T + d * np.eye(d)

mU, mV = rng.normal(size=d), rng.normal(size=d)
SU, SV = rand_cov(), rand_cov()

S  = np.real(sqrtm(SU))
Si = np.linalg.inv(S)
M  = np.real(sqrtm(S @ SV @ S))
A  = Si @ M @ Si                                  # equation (gaussian-map)

print(np.allclose(A, A.T))                        # True: A is symmetric
print(np.linalg.eigvalsh(A).min() > 0)            # True: A is positive definite
print(np.allclose(A @ SU @ A, SV))                # True: pushes mu to nu

w2 = np.sum((mU - mV) ** 2) + np.trace(SU + SV - 2 * M)
u  = rng.multivariate_normal(mU, SU, 400_000)
t  = mV + (u - mU) @ A.T                          # A symmetric, so A.T == A
print(w2, np.mean(np.sum((u - t) ** 2, axis=1)))  # the two agree
```

## Back to generative models {#sec-synthesis}

We can now close the loop opened in @sec-why. A generator defines
$\mu_{\theta} = G_{\theta \#}\nu$ by @eq-generator-pushforward, and training
means minimising some discrepancy $D(\mu_{\theta}, p_{\text{data}})$ over
$\theta$. This chapter has supplied two families of candidates for $D$, and the
choice between them is an optimisation decision rather than a matter of taste.

Take $D$ to be an $f$-divergence and one obtains the adversarial models. The
original GAN objective, at its optimal discriminator, reduces to the
Jensen--Shannon divergence between $\mu_{\theta}$ and $p_{\text{data}}$ up to an
additive constant; $f$-GAN generalises this by replacing the generator $f$ and
deriving the corresponding variational bound. @thm-saturation is then the
warning label on the whole construction: as soon as the discriminator becomes
good enough to separate the two supports, the objective is pinned at
$f(0) + f'(\infty)$ and its gradient in $\theta$ vanishes.

Take $D$ to be an integral probability metric and one obtains the alternatives.
W-GAN takes $\mathcal{F} = \mathrm{Lip}_{1}$ and optimises the dual in
@eq-kr, which is why its critic is Lipschitz-constrained and why its loss
remains informative when the supports are disjoint --- by
@exm-parallel-lines it still reports $\lvert \theta \rvert$. The general statement behind that
example --- that the loss is continuous in $\theta$, where the Jensen--Shannon
one is not --- is @sec-adv-continuity. McGAN and MMD-GAN
take $\mathcal{F}$ to be a moment class or an RKHS ball and use
@eq-mmd-expanded, which is estimable directly from two samples and needs no
inner maximisation at all.

| Discrepancy | Metric | Needs $P \ll Q$ | Value when $P \perp Q$ | Used by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $D_{\mathrm{KL}}$ | no | yes | $+\infty$ | maximum likelihood |
| Reverse $D_{\mathrm{KL}}$ | no | yes | $+\infty$ | variational inference |
| $D_{\mathrm{JS}}$ | no | no | $\log 2$ | GAN, $f$-GAN |
| Total variation | yes | no | $1$ | analysis, rarely trained |
| $\mathrm{MMD}$ | yes | no | varies with the kernel | MMD-GAN, McGAN |
