| $W_{1}$ | yes | no | varies with the distance | W-GAN |

The last two rows are the point of the table. Only for the integral
probability metrics does the entry in the fourth column depend on the
configuration of the two distributions rather than on the discrepancy alone,
and that dependence is precisely the gradient signal a generator needs.
@fig-map collects the whole development onto one page.

![The two routes from a statistical distance to a generative model. Reading
down the left branch gives the adversarial family and its saturation problem;
reading down the right gives the transport and moment-matching families.
Kantorovich--Rubinstein duality, @eq-kr, is the bridge between the two
branches.](figures/lec01/jungwoo-ahn-fig8.png){#fig-map width=85%}

Three threads continue directly into the next lectures. The reduction of the
GAN objective to the Jensen--Shannon divergence, and the $f$-GAN variational
bound, are the subject of Lecture 02, as are W-GAN, McGAN and the geometric
view. @eq-adain, the optimal map between isotropic Gaussians, returns as the
adaptive instance normalisation layer of StyleGAN in Lecture 03. And the idea
that a generative model is a transport of one measure onto another --- rather
than a likelihood to be maximised --- is the thread that runs through the
diffusion, flow matching and Schrodinger bridge lectures in the rest of the
course.

## Advanced topics {#sec-advanced}

The chapter above follows the lecture. This section collects material that the
lecture did not cover but that the development above leans on or leaves
open: a divergence the tables list without evaluating, the two estimators that
make the maximum mean discrepancy usable, the linear-programming form of the
Kantorovich problem, the hypotheses under which duality survives the passage to
Polish spaces, and the topological facts that turn @exm-parallel-lines from an
example into a theorem about training. Each subsection is self-contained and
none is needed to follow the main line.

### Where the Pearson chi-squared divergence is finite {#sec-adv-chi2}

The generator table of @sec-f-divergences lists $f(u) = (u-1)^{2}$, and the
saturation table of @sec-saturation gives its row, but neither is worked
through in the chapter. Here $f(0) = 1$ and
$f'(\infty) = \lim_{u \to \infty} (u-1)^{2}/u = +\infty$, so by
@thm-saturation the Pearson $\chi^{2}$ divergence is $+\infty$ on mutually
singular pairs, joining the two Kullback--Leibler divergences rather than the
bounded generators.

Away from that case,

$$
D_{\chi^{2}}(P \Vert Q)
  = \int \left( \frac{dP}{dQ} - 1 \right)^{2} dQ
  = \int \left( \frac{dP}{dQ} \right)^{2} dQ \; - \; 1 ,
$$ {#eq-chi-squared}

so $\chi^{2}$ is finite exactly when $P \ll Q$ **and** $dP/dQ \in L^{2}(Q)$.
That is a strictly stronger demand than the absolute continuity
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}$ needs, and it is why $\chi^{2}$ plays no part in the
generative models of this course: the situation of @sec-saturation defeats it
even more thoroughly than the others.

### How literal is the dual-norm reading? {#sec-adv-dualnorm}

@def-ipm was introduced as the norm of the signed measure $\mu - \nu$
measured over a unit ball. The reading is exact for two of the three classes of
@sec-ipm and only approximate for the third, and the difference is worth
pinning down because it is the reason
@thm-kantorovich-rubinstein needs a normalisation.

If $\lVert \cdot \rVert_{B}$ is a genuine norm on a space $B$ of test
functions and $\mathcal{F} = \{ h : \lVert h \rVert_{B} \leq 1 \}$, then

$$
d_{\mathcal{F}}(\mu,\nu) = \lVert \mu - \nu \rVert_{B^{\ast}}
$$ {#eq-ipm-dual-norm}

by the definition of the dual norm. The indicator class and the RKHS ball of
@prp-mmd are of this kind. The class $\mathrm{Lip}_{1}$ is not: the Lipschitz
constant vanishes on constant functions, so it is a seminorm rather than a
norm, and $\mathrm{Lip}_{1}$ is unbounded in any function norm --- it contains
$\varphi + t$ for every real $t$. The dual reading is recovered by quotienting
out the constants, which is legitimate here because $\mu - \nu$ annihilates
them, both measures having total mass $1$; equivalently, by normalising
$\varphi(x_{0}) = 0$ at a base point, which is what one does in practice when
implementing @eq-kr.

The choice of $\mathcal{F}$ also fixes a topology on $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})$,
and the three are genuinely different:

| $\mathcal{F}$ | Metric | Topology induced |
|---|---|---|
| indicators $\mathbf{1}_{A}$ | total variation | strictly finer than weak; the one @thm-saturation bites in |
| $\{ h : \lVert h \rVert_{\infty} + \mathrm{Lip}(h) \leq 1 \}$ | bounded-Lipschitz | weak convergence |
| $\mathrm{Lip}_{1}$ | $W_{1}$ | weak convergence, on a space of bounded diameter |

The second row is the Dudley metric. The third is what @sec-adv-topology takes
up in general, and the gap between the first row and the other two is the whole
argument of @sec-synthesis.

### Estimating the maximum mean discrepancy {#sec-adv-mmd}

@eq-mmd-expanded writes $\mathrm{MMD}^{2}$ entirely in terms of expectations
of the kernel, which is what makes it usable: no density estimate and no inner
maximisation. Given $x_{1},\dots,x_{m} \sim \mu$ and
$y_{1},\dots,y_{n} \sim \nu$ independently, replacing each expectation by the
corresponding sample average gives the $V$-statistic

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{MMD}}^{2}_{V}
  = \frac{1}{m^{2}} \sum_{i,j} k(x_{i},x_{j})
  - \frac{2}{mn} \sum_{i,j} k(x_{i},y_{j})
  + \frac{1}{n^{2}} \sum_{i,j} k(y_{i},y_{j}) .
$$ {#eq-mmd-v}

It is biased upwards, because the diagonal terms $k(x_{i},x_{i})$ estimate
$\mathbb{E}_{x,x'}k(x,x')$ with $x' = x$ rather than with an independent copy.
Deleting the diagonals gives the $U$-statistic

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{MMD}}^{2}_{U}
  = \frac{1}{m(m-1)} \sum_{i \neq j} k(x_{i},x_{j})
  - \frac{2}{mn} \sum_{i,j} k(x_{i},y_{j})
  + \frac{1}{n(n-1)} \sum_{i \neq j} k(y_{i},y_{j}) ,
$$ {#eq-mmd-u}

which is unbiased for $\mathrm{MMD}^{2}$ but is no longer a squared norm, so a
single estimate can come out negative when the two distributions agree. Both
need $O\bigl((m+n)^{2}\bigr)$ kernel evaluations. That quadratic cost is what
keeps the maximum mean discrepancy to moderate batch sizes, and is the
practical reason it is more often used as a two-sample *test* statistic than as
a training loss at scale.

Whether the maximum mean discrepancy separates distributions at all is a
property of the kernel and not of the estimator. Call $k$ **characteristic** if
the mean embedding $\mu \mapsto m_{\mu}$ is injective on
$\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})$; by @prp-ipm-metric this is exactly the condition
under which $\mathrm{MMD}(\mu,\nu) = 0$ if and only if $\mu = \nu$, that is,
under which @eq-mmd is a metric and not merely a pseudo-metric. For a
translation-invariant kernel on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ the condition can be read off
the spectrum. Bochner's theorem writes

$$
k(x,y) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}
  e^{i \langle \omega, \, x-y \rangle} \, d\Lambda(\omega)
$$ {#eq-bochner}

for a finite non-negative spectral measure $\Lambda$, and $k$ is characteristic
exactly when $\mathrm{supp}(\Lambda) = \mathbb{R}^{d}$: the embedding then sees
every frequency of the characteristic function of $\mu - \nu$, so no non-zero
difference can be invisible. The Gaussian kernel qualifies, its spectral
measure being Gaussian and hence of full support. A band-limited kernel does
not, and is blind to whatever the two distributions do above its cutoff.

### The topology of the Wasserstein distance {#sec-adv-topology}

@thm-wp-metric establishes that $W_{p}$ is a metric. That alone is not the
property @sec-synthesis relies on; what matters is which notion of convergence
it defines. On a Polish space,

$$
W_{p}(\mu_{n},\mu) \to 0
\iff
\mu_{n} \to \mu \ \text{weakly}
\ \ \text{and} \ \
\int d(x,x_{0})^{p} d\mu_{n} \to \int d(x,x_{0})^{p} d\mu
$$ {#eq-wp-topology}

for some --- equivalently any --- base point $x_{0}$. On a space of bounded
diameter, which is the case for images confined to a fixed pixel range, the
moment condition is automatic and $W_{p}$ metrises weak convergence outright.

No $f$-divergence does this. Total variation and the Jensen--Shannon
divergence induce a strictly finer topology, and @exm-parallel-lines is the gap
made concrete: $\mu_{\theta} \to \mu_{0}$ weakly as $\theta \to 0$, yet both
stay pinned at their saturation values until the instant $\theta = 0$. That
mismatch of topologies, rather than the arithmetic of any single example, is
the precise sense in which the Wasserstein distance "still varies smoothly"
where the others do not, and @sec-adv-continuity turns it into a statement
about training.

### Two further ways Monge's problem fails {#sec-adv-monge}

@prp-monge-fails rules out a transport map by an atom: a map cannot split
mass. It is easy to read that as the only difficulty, and to conclude that a
non-atomic $\mu$ makes @eq-monge well behaved. It does not. The feasible set
$\{T : T_{\#}\mu = \nu\}$ is not closed in any topology for which $\mathbb{M}$
is continuous, so the infimum can fail to be attained even when feasible maps
are plentiful.

::: {#exm-monge-not-attained}
## An infimum with no minimiser
Work in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ with $c(x,y) = \lVert x-y \rVert$. Let $\mu$ be
uniform on the segment $\{0\} \times [0,1]$, and let
$\nu = \tfrac{1}{2}\nu_{-} + \tfrac{1}{2}\nu_{+}$ with $\nu_{\pm}$ uniform
on $\{\pm 1\} \times [0,1]$. Then $\inf_{T} \mathbb{M}(T) = 1$, but
$\mathbb{M}(T) > 1$ for every feasible $T$, so no optimal map exists.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Every feasible map costs more than $1$.* A point $x = (0,t)$ and a point
$y = (\pm 1, s)$ of the target are at distance
$\sqrt{1 + (t-s)^{2}} \geq 1$, with equality only when $s = t$. So
$\mathbb{M}(T) \geq 1$ always, with equality only if $T$ preserves height
$\mu$-almost everywhere. But a height-preserving $T$ pushes $\mu$ onto a set
meeting each height at most once, whereas $\nu$ charges two points at every
height; such a $T$ is not feasible. Hence $\mathbb{M}(T) > 1$.

*The infimum is $1$.* Cut $[0,1]$ into $2n$ strips of height $1/(2n)$ and let
$T_{n}$ send the odd strips to the left target and the even strips to the
right, each by the affine map onto the corresponding strip of height $1/n$.
Each half receives mass $n \cdot \tfrac{1}{2n} = \tfrac{1}{2}$ spread
uniformly, so $T_{n}$ is feasible, and it moves any point vertically by at most
$1/n$, so $\mathbb{M}(T_{n}) \leq \sqrt{1 + n^{-2}} \to 1$.

*Kantorovich attains it.* The plan that splits each $(0,t)$ evenly between
$(-1,t)$ and $(1,t)$ is a coupling of cost exactly $1$.
:::

This example also sharpens @eq-relaxation: there the inequality is strict with
*both* sides finite, which @prp-monge-fails, whose right-hand side is an
infimum over the empty set, could not show.

Failure of uniqueness is a third phenomenon, independent of the other two. For
Monge's original cost $c(x,y) = \lVert x-y \rVert$, take
$\mu = \mathrm{Uniform}[0,1]$ and $\nu = \mathrm{Uniform}[2,3]$ on the line.
Every target point lies to the right of every source point, so
$\lvert x-y \rvert = y-x$ and every feasible map has the same cost
$\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[y] - \mathbb{E}_{\mu}[x] = 2$. All of them are optimal,
including the monotone map of @thm-monge-1d and including maps that reverse
order. Uniqueness, when it holds, comes from strict convexity of the cost ---
it is the quadratic cost of @thm-brenier that forces a single answer, not
transport as such.

### The Kantorovich problem as a linear program {#sec-adv-lp}

On finite spaces @eq-kantorovich is a linear program, and it is worth
displaying rather than leaving inside the proof of @thm-kantorovich-duality: it
is what a solver actually receives, and its shape is the reason the dual of
@sec-duality, and not the primal, is what generative models implement. Take
$\mathcal{X} = \{x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\}$ and
$\mathcal{Y} = \{y_{1},\dots,y_{n}\}$, collect the marginals into vectors
$\mu \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and $\nu \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and the costs into the
matrix $C_{ij} = c(x_{i},y_{j})$. A coupling is a matrix
$\Pi \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ and @eq-kantorovich reads

$$
\min_{\Pi \geq 0} \; \langle C, \Pi \rangle = \sum_{i,j} C_{ij}\Pi_{ij}
\qquad \text{subject to} \qquad
\Pi \mathbf{1}_{n} = \mu , \quad \Pi^{\top} \mathbf{1}_{m} = \nu .
$$ {#eq-kantorovich-lp}

The feasible set of @eq-kantorovich-lp is the transportation polytope of $\mu$
and $\nu$: non-empty, compact and convex. It carries $mn$ non-negative
variables against only $m+n$ equality constraints, one of which is redundant,
since summing either family returns the total mass $1$; so $m+n-1$ are
independent. That imbalance is the whole of computational optimal transport.
The primal holds a variable for every *pair* of points, the dual of
@sec-duality one per point, and once $m$ and $n$ reach the tens of thousands
only the second can be stored at all.

The polytope also settles when Monge and Kantorovich agree. Suppose $m = n$ and
both marginals are uniform, $\mu = \nu = \tfrac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}_{n}$. The
feasible set is then $\tfrac{1}{n}\mathcal{B}_{n}$, where $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ is
the Birkhoff polytope of doubly stochastic matrices. By the Birkhoff--von
Neumann theorem the extreme points of $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ are exactly the
permutation matrices, and a linear objective on a compact convex polytope
attains its minimum at an extreme point. So an optimal plan may be taken to be
$\tfrac{1}{n}P_{\sigma}$ for a permutation $\sigma$ --- that is, to be induced
by a map after all, and @eq-relaxation holds with equality. The relaxation
costs nothing for discrete measures with equal atom weights; it earns its keep
in the unequal and continuous cases, which are the ones
@prp-monge-fails and @exm-monge-not-attained describe.

![A plan $\Pi$ drawn as a weighted bipartite graph, which is what
@eq-kantorovich-lp is. **A.** The obstruction of @prp-monge-fails: the single
source atom has to send mass to two targets, and only an edge weight can do
that. **B.** A plan between $\mu$ with mass $\tfrac{1}{2}$ at $0$ and $2$ and
$\nu$ with masses $\tfrac{1}{4}, \tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{4}$ at $0, 1, 2$.
Each edge carries one entry $\Pi_{ij}$; the edges leaving a source sum to its
mass and those entering a target sum to its, which are the two marginal
constraints. For $c = \lvert x-y \rvert$ this plan costs
$\tfrac{1}{4}\cdot 0 + \tfrac{1}{4}\cdot 1 + \tfrac{1}{4}\cdot 1 +
\tfrac{1}{4}\cdot 0 = \tfrac{1}{2}$, which is
$W_{1}$.](figures/lec01/swy99-couplings.png){#fig-couplings width=95%}

### Duality beyond finite spaces {#sec-adv-duality}

The proof of @thm-kantorovich-duality settles strong duality on finite spaces
and defers the rest to a citation. Two things that citation hides are worth
stating; a consequence for the optimal plans themselves follows in
@sec-adv-slackness.

*What the general theorem needs.* Strong duality in @eq-ot-duality holds whenever
$\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ are Polish and $c$ is lower semicontinuous and
bounded below. Neither continuity of $c$ nor finiteness of the optimal value is
required. The proof is not a limit of the finite argument above; it is a
Fenchel--Rockafellar duality in the pair
$\bigl( C_{b}(\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}),
\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}) \bigr)$, with the lower
semicontinuous $c$ approached from below by bounded continuous costs.

*When the supremum is attained.* @eq-ot-duality is written with a supremum and not
a maximum deliberately: optimal potentials need not exist. They do exist, and
are then called Kantorovich potentials as in @def-c-transform, under a mild
domination hypothesis --- it is enough that $c$ be continuous and that
$c(x,y) \leq a(x) + b(y)$ for some $a \in L^{1}(\mu)$ and $b \in L^{1}(\nu)$.
Both costs used in this chapter satisfy it whenever the measures have the
moments @def-wasserstein assumes, since
$\lVert x-y \rVert \leq \lVert x \rVert + \lVert y \rVert$ and
$\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert x-y \rVert^{2} \leq \lVert x \rVert^{2} + \lVert y
\rVert^{2}$. This is the hypothesis that licenses @thm-brenier to begin by
taking optimal potentials as given.

### Complementary slackness and cyclical monotonicity {#sec-adv-slackness}

Duality constrains the optimal plans themselves and not only the optimal value.
The weak-duality computation in @thm-kantorovich-duality integrated an
inequality; once the two optimal values agree, that inequality has nowhere left
to hide.

::: {#prp-complementary-slackness}
## Complementary slackness
Let $\pi$ be optimal for @eq-kantorovich and $(\varphi,\psi)$ optimal for
@eq-ot-duality, with the common value finite. Then

$$
\varphi(x) + \psi(y) = c(x,y)
\qquad \text{for } \pi\text{-almost every } (x,y) ,
$$ {#eq-slackness}

so $\pi$ is concentrated on the set where the dual constraint is active. When
$\psi = \varphi^{c}$, that set is the $c$-superdifferential of $\varphi$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The function $c(x,y) - \varphi(x) - \psi(y)$ is non-negative by the definition
of $\Phi_{c}$, and its integral against $\pi$ is
$\mathbb{K}(\pi) - \mathbb{J}(\varphi,\psi)$, which vanishes by @eq-ot-duality. A
non-negative function with zero integral is zero almost everywhere.
:::

@eq-slackness is the engine of every structural result about optimal plans; it
is what @thm-brenier uses to turn a coupling into a map. It also has a
consequence that mentions no potentials at all. If $\pi$ is optimal then
$\mathrm{supp}(\pi)$ is **$c$-cyclically monotone**: for every finite family
$(x_{1},y_{1}),\dots,(x_{N},y_{N})$ in the support and every permutation
$\sigma$ of $\{1,\dots,N\}$,

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{N} c(x_{i},y_{i})
  \; \leq \; \sum_{i=1}^{N} c\bigl( x_{i}, y_{\sigma(i)} \bigr) .
$$ {#eq-cyclical-monotonicity}

The proof is one line from @eq-slackness: summing the equality over the family
gives $\sum_{i} c(x_{i},y_{i}) = \sum_{i}\varphi(x_{i}) + \sum_{i}\psi(y_{i})$,
the right-hand side is unchanged by reindexing $\psi$ along $\sigma$, and
$\varphi(x_{i}) + \psi(y_{\sigma(i)}) \leq c(x_{i},y_{\sigma(i)})$ term by
term. In words: no finite reshuffling of destinations among the pairs the plan
actually uses can lower the bill. For $c$ continuous and real-valued the
converse holds as well --- a coupling with $c$-cyclically monotone support is
optimal --- so @eq-cyclical-monotonicity characterises optimality with no
reference to the dual problem.

### The c-transform for the quadratic cost {#sec-adv-legendre}

For $c(x,y) = \lVert x-y \rVert$ the $c$-transform of a $1$-Lipschitz
function is simply its negative, which is @lem-ctransform-lipschitz. For the
quadratic cost it is the Legendre transform wearing a disguise, and that
identification is the whole of the change of variables in @thm-brenier.

$c(x,y) = \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert x-y \rVert^{2}$ the $c$-transform is the Legendre
transform wearing a disguise. Put
$u(x) = \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert x \rVert^{2} - \varphi(x)$ and expand the square:

$$
\varphi^{c}(y)
  = \inf_{x} \Bigl\{ \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert x-y \rVert^{2} - \varphi(x) \Bigr\}
  = \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert y \rVert^{2}
    - \sup_{x} \bigl\{ \langle x,y \rangle - u(x) \bigr\}
  = \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert y \rVert^{2} - u^{\ast}(y) .
$$ {#eq-c-transform-quadratic}

So $\varphi$ is $c$-concave for the quadratic cost exactly when
$u = \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert \cdot \rVert^{2} - \varphi$ is convex and lower
semicontinuous: applying @eq-c-transform-quadratic twice turns $c$-concavity of
$\varphi$ into the identity $u = u^{\ast\ast}$, which is the Fenchel--Moreau
theorem. It is worth registering that what appears is *convexity* of $u$ and
not concavity --- the $c$-transform reverses order, and the
$\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert \cdot \rVert^{2}$ absorbs the sign. This identification is
the entire change of variables of @thm-brenier, which carries it out in a
single line.

### Continuity of the Wasserstein loss {#sec-adv-continuity}

@exm-parallel-lines shows one generator, with one parameter, on which $W_{1}$
carries a gradient and the $f$-divergences do not. The general statement rests
on @sec-adv-topology: $W_{1}$ metrises weak convergence on a space of bounded
diameter, whereas total variation and the Jensen--Shannon divergence induce a
strictly finer topology.

Suppose $G_{\theta}(z)$ is locally Lipschitz in $\theta$, uniformly in $z$ up
to an integrable envelope --- a condition any feed-forward network with
Lipschitz activations satisfies. Then $\theta \mapsto \mu_{\theta}$ is
continuous for weak convergence, so by @eq-wp-topology

$$
\theta \mapsto W_{1}(\mu_{\theta}, p_{\text{data}})
$$ {#eq-w1-in-theta}

is continuous everywhere and, being locally Lipschitz, differentiable almost
everywhere. Gradient descent on it is therefore well posed wherever it is run.

No such statement is available for $D_{\mathrm{JS}}$. By @thm-saturation it is
locally constant wherever the supports separate, which by the dimension count
of @sec-saturation is essentially everywhere; it is differentiable almost
everywhere too, but with derivative zero, which is worse than useless. This is
Theorem 1 of Arjovsky, Chintala and Bottou, and it is the reason the loss was
worth changing.


## Appendix: proof of the Radon--Nikodym theorem {#sec-appendix-rn}

@thm-radon-nikodym was used throughout without proof. The following argument,
due to von Neumann, is short and uses only the Riesz representation theorem in
a Hilbert space, so it is worth including rather than citing.

::: {.proof}
Assume first that $\lambda$ and $\nu$ are finite, with $\lambda \ll \nu$, and
set $\rho = \lambda + \nu$, also finite. Consider the linear functional

$$
L(f) = \int_{\Omega} f \, d\lambda , \qquad f \in L^{2}(\rho) .
$$

It is bounded: by Cauchy--Schwarz in $L^{2}(\rho)$, and since
$\lambda \leq \rho$,

$$
\lvert L(f) \rvert \leq \int \lvert f \rvert \, d\lambda
  \leq \int \lvert f \rvert \, d\rho
  \leq \lVert f \rVert_{L^{2}(\rho)} \, \rho(\Omega)^{1/2} .
$$

By the Riesz representation theorem there is $g \in L^{2}(\rho)$ with

$$
\int f \, d\lambda = \int f g \, d\rho
  = \int f g \, d\lambda + \int f g \, d\nu
\qquad \text{for all } f \in L^{2}(\rho) ,
$$

and rearranging,

$$
\int f \, (1 - g) \, d\lambda = \int f g \, d\nu .
$$ {#eq-rn-key}

Taking $f = \mathbf{1}_{\{g < 0\}}$ in $\int f d\lambda = \int fg \, d\rho$
forces $\rho(\{g<0\}) = 0$, and taking $f = \mathbf{1}_{\{g>1\}}$ gives
$\int_{\{g>1\}} (1-g) \, d\lambda = \int_{\{g>1\}} g \, d\nu \geq 0$ with a
strictly negative left-hand side unless $\rho(\{g>1\}) = 0$. So
$0 \leq g \leq 1$ $\rho$-almost everywhere.

Let $N = \{ g = 1 \}$. Taking $f = \mathbf{1}_{N}$ in @eq-rn-key gives
$0 = \nu(N)$, and since $\lambda \ll \nu$ also $\lambda(N) = 0$.

Now fix a measurable $A$ and take
$f = \mathbf{1}_{A}\bigl( 1 + g + \cdots + g^{n-1} \bigr)$ in @eq-rn-key. The
left-hand side telescopes, since $(1 + \cdots + g^{n-1})(1-g) = 1 - g^{n}$:

$$
\int_{A} \bigl( 1 - g^{n} \bigr) d\lambda
  = \int_{A} \bigl( g + g^{2} + \cdots + g^{n} \bigr) d\nu .
$$

Let $n \to \infty$. On $\{g < 1\}$ we have $g^{n} \to 0$, and $\lambda(N) = 0$,
so the left side tends to $\lambda(A)$ by dominated convergence. The right side
increases to $\int_{A} \sum_{k \geq 1} g^{k} \, d\nu
= \int_{A} \frac{g}{1-g} \, d\nu$ by monotone convergence, the integrand being
defined $\nu$-almost everywhere because $\nu(N) = 0$. Hence

$$
\lambda(A) = \int_{A} h \, d\nu , \qquad h = \frac{g}{1-g} \geq 0 ,
$$

which is @eq-radon-nikodym. For $\sigma$-finite measures, partition $\Omega$
into countably many sets of finite measure and add the resulting densities.

Uniqueness: if $\int_{A} h_{1} d\nu = \int_{A} h_{2} d\nu$ for every $A$, then
taking $A = \{h_{1} > h_{2}\}$ and $A = \{h_{1} < h_{2}\}$ in turn forces both
sets to be $\nu$-null, so $h_{1} = h_{2}$ $\nu$-almost everywhere.
:::
